name: Bitcoin
summary: The first cryptocurrency network: a proof-of-work blockchain for sending and holding bitcoin (BTC) without a central operator.
goodToKnow: Bitcoin's scripting language is deliberately limited; it does not run general-purpose smart contracts the way Ethereum does.
"Bitcoin" can mean the network/protocol or the BTC currency unit; Bitcoin Core is the main software implementation, not the network itself.

detail.whatItIs: Bitcoin is the first cryptocurrency, launched in January 2009 by the pseudonymous Satoshi Nakamoto. It lets people send and hold bitcoin (BTC) directly, without a bank or company in the middle. People use it to store value and to make payments, sometimes through layers built on it, such as the Lightning Network. No one owns the network: anyone can run a node, volunteers maintain its main software, and rule changes need broad agreement among users, miners and developers. It is the original Layer 1 blockchain.
detail.howItWorks: Bitcoin uses proof of work. Miners repeatedly hash a candidate block until the result falls below a target, which takes about ten minutes on average; the difficulty adjusts every 2,016 blocks to keep that pace. The winner earns newly issued bitcoin, an amount that halves about every four years, plus transaction fees. Nodes follow the valid chain with the most accumulated work. Balances are unspent transaction outputs (UTXOs): each payment spends earlier outputs and creates new ones, each locked by a short script that usually requires a signature. Total supply is capped at 21 million BTC.

name: Ethereum
summary: Proof-of-stake blockchain that runs smart contracts on the EVM; it also serves as the settlement layer for many rollups.
goodToKnow: Ethereum switched from proof of work to proof of stake in September 2022 ("the Merge").
ETH is the native asset used to pay transaction fees (gas); "Ethereum" is the network.
Many L2 rollups post their data and proofs to Ethereum, which is why it sits at the centre of the Ethereum ecosystem.

detail.whatItIs: Ethereum is a public blockchain that runs smart contracts: programs that anyone can deploy and anyone can call. Its native coin, ETH, pays transaction fees and is staked to secure the network. Many stablecoins, lending and trading protocols started on Ethereum, and dozens of Layer 2 networks use it as the chain where their transactions are finally settled. No company runs it: independent teams build its client software, and changes are agreed in public calls between client developers and researchers.
detail.howItWorks: Since the Merge in September 2022, Ethereum uses proof of stake. Validators lock ETH; every 12 seconds one is chosen to propose a block and committees of others vote on it. A block becomes final after about 13 minutes, after which reverting it would destroy a large share of the staked ETH. Since the Pectra upgrade in May 2025, one validator can hold from 32 up to 2,048 ETH. Transactions run in the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM), where every step costs gas. Rollups post data in blobs, and since Fusaka in December 2025 nodes check only samples of each blob.

name: Solana
summary: Proof-of-stake layer-1 blockchain designed for high throughput, running transactions in parallel with its own virtual machine (SVM).
goodToKnow: Transactions declare in advance which accounts they read and write, which lets the runtime execute non-conflicting ones in parallel.
Solana programs are not EVM contracts: Ethereum tools and addresses do not work there directly.
The network has had several full outages in the past (between 2021 and 2024).

detail.whatItIs: Solana is a public blockchain designed to process many transactions quickly and cheaply. People use it for payments, stablecoin transfers, token trading, NFTs and other apps. Its native coin, SOL, pays fees and is staked to secure the network. No company runs it: independent validators operate the network, using validator software from more than one team, such as Anza's Agave and Jump Crypto's Firedancer. The Solana Foundation, a Swiss non-profit, funds ecosystem work. It is a Layer 1, a base chain that does not settle on another chain.
detail.howItWorks: Solana uses proof of stake. A schedule published in advance names the validator that leads each slot of about 400 milliseconds and produces its block. Since October 2026, validators agree on blocks with Votor, part of the Alpenglow upgrade, which replaced the older TowerBFT voting. Votes travel directly between validators instead of as on-chain transactions, and a block can be final after one round if 80% of stake approves, or after two rounds otherwise. The Sealevel runtime then executes transactions that touch different accounts at the same time.

name: BNB Chain
summary: Blockchain ecosystem started by Binance; its main network, BNB Smart Chain, is an EVM-compatible chain paying fees in BNB.
goodToKnow: BNB Smart Chain uses a small, permissioned-by-stake validator set (Proof of Staked Authority), trading decentralisation for low fees and speed.
BNB Chain also includes opBNB (an L2) and BNB Greenfield (storage); the older BNB Beacon Chain was shut down in 2024.
Many tokens on BNB Smart Chain are "Binance-Peg" versions of assets from other chains, issued by Binance rather than the original issuer.

detail.whatItIs: BNB Chain is a group of blockchains that Binance started in 2020 and still supports. Its main network, BNB Smart Chain, runs the same kind of smart contracts as Ethereum, so Ethereum wallets and Solidity code work with little change. People use it for low-fee token trading, stablecoin transfers and games. BNB, the native coin, pays fees and is staked to secure the network. The ecosystem also includes opBNB, a Layer 2 for cheaper transactions, and BNB Greenfield for data storage. BNB Smart Chain itself is a Layer 1.
detail.howItWorks: BNB Smart Chain uses Proof of Staked Authority, a mix of proof of stake and a small set of approved block producers. BNB holders delegate stake to validator candidates, and those with the most stake form the active set, which takes turns producing blocks. Since the Fermi hard fork in January 2026, a block arrives about every 0.45 seconds, and validators vote on blocks so that one is usually final within a few blocks. Contracts run in the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM); gas is paid in BNB, and part of each fee is burned.

sources.label: BNB Chain blog: Fermi hard fork

name: Avalanche
summary: Proof-of-stake network of interoperable chains; its C-Chain runs EVM smart contracts and others can launch their own Avalanche L1s.
goodToKnow: The primary network has three chains: C-Chain (smart contracts), X-Chain (asset transfers) and P-Chain (validators and L1 management).
"Subnets" were renamed "Avalanche L1s" in the Avalanche9000 upgrade (December 2024); older articles use the old name.

detail.whatItIs: Avalanche is a public proof-of-stake network made up of several connected blockchains. Most users meet it through the C-Chain, which runs Ethereum-style smart contracts and hosts lending, trading and stablecoin apps. Its token, AVAX, pays fees and is staked by validators. Companies and communities can also launch their own Avalanche L1s: separate chains with their own rules, fees and validators that can still exchange messages with other Avalanche chains. Ava Labs writes much of the core software, and the Avalanche Foundation supports the ecosystem.
detail.howItWorks: Avalanche consensus works by repeated random sampling. Each validator asks a small random group of other validators which block they prefer, adopts the majority answer, and repeats until the answer stays the same for enough rounds in a row. The chains use Snowman, a version of this protocol for chains with a single line of blocks, so a block is final once sampling settles, with no need to wait for later blocks. Since the Avalanche9000 upgrade in December 2024, validators of an Avalanche L1 pay a continuous AVAX fee instead of also staking on the primary network.

name: Cardano
summary: Proof-of-stake layer-1 blockchain using the Ouroboros protocol and an extended UTXO model for its native ADA and smart contracts.
goodToKnow: Cardano uses an extended UTXO (eUTXO) model, closer to Bitcoin's than to Ethereum's account model, so contracts are written differently.
Its protocol design is developed through peer-reviewed research, and on-chain governance (CIP-1694) lets ADA holders vote on changes.

detail.whatItIs: Cardano is a public proof-of-stake blockchain with its own coin, ADA, used for payments, fees and staking. It also runs smart contracts for lending, trading and other apps. Charles Hoskinson, a co-founder of Ethereum, started it in 2015, and three organisations built it: Input Output, EMURGO and the Cardano Foundation. Since the Plomin upgrade in January 2025, ADA holders, elected representatives and a constitutional committee govern changes on-chain under a written constitution. Independent stake pool operators run the network. It is a Layer 1.
detail.howItWorks: Cardano's consensus protocol, Ouroboros Praos, divides time into one-second slots grouped into five-day epochs. In each slot, every stake pool privately runs a verifiable random function; a pool wins the right to make a block with a probability proportional to its stake, which gives roughly one block every 20 seconds. ADA holders delegate to a pool without locking their coins or handing them over. Transactions spend existing outputs and create new ones, and a Plutus script attached to an output decides whether a transaction may spend it.

name: IOTA
summary: Layer-1 network that started as a DAG "Tangle" ledger and, since its 2025 Rebased upgrade, is a validator-run proof-of-stake chain.
goodToKnow: The "Rebased" upgrade (mainnet 5 May 2025) replaced the original Tangle design. The hub's DAG demo shows that historical Tangle design, not today's IOTA.
As of November 2026: an object-based ledger with Move smart contracts, run by a delegated proof-of-stake validator committee using Starfish consensus.
Starfish (enabled on mainnet in 2026) succeeds Mysticeti; it is a DAG-based protocol among validators, unlike the old Tangle of user transactions.

detail.whatItIs: IOTA is a public blockchain that started in 2016 as an experiment in feeless payments between connected devices, built on a structure called the Tangle. Since the Rebased upgrade in May 2025 it works much like other modern proof-of-stake chains: validators run it, smart contracts are written in Move, and transactions pay small fees in the IOTA token. The IOTA Foundation, a non-profit, develops it and focuses on uses such as trade documents, digital identity and tokenised assets. It is a Layer 1.
detail.howItWorks: Rebased IOTA reuses much of Sui's open-source design. Everything on the ledger is an object with an owner, and Move contracts define what can be done with each object. IOTA holders delegate tokens to validators, and a committee chosen by stake stays fixed for each epoch of about one day. The committee orders transactions with Starfish: each validator keeps publishing blocks that reference other validators' blocks, forming a shared graph, and parts of that graph are committed once enough validators have referenced them. Validators share their epoch rewards with delegators.

name: Cosmos Hub
summary: Proof-of-stake blockchain at the centre of the Cosmos ecosystem, connected to other Cosmos SDK chains through IBC.
goodToKnow: "Cosmos" usually means the whole ecosystem of independent chains built with the Cosmos SDK; the Cosmos Hub is just one of them.
Its native token is ATOM; the Hub's node software is called Gaia.

detail.whatItIs: The Cosmos Hub is the first blockchain launched in the Cosmos ecosystem, live since March 2019. It is a proof-of-stake Layer 1 whose token, ATOM, is used for staking, fees and governance. It acts as a meeting point for other independent Cosmos chains, which connect to it through IBC to move tokens and messages. The Hub has no single owner: ATOM stakers vote on-chain on software upgrades and on spending from its community pool, and independent teams maintain its node software, Gaia.
detail.howItWorks: The Hub runs CometBFT consensus. A limited active set of validators, chosen by how much ATOM is staked with them, take turns proposing blocks every few seconds, and a block is final once validators holding over two-thirds of the stake sign it. ATOM holders delegate to validators and share their rewards. Misbehaviour such as double-signing is punished by slashing part of the stake, and unstaking takes 21 days. In 2026 governance began winding down Interchain Security, a system that let Hub validators also secure other chains.

name: Osmosis
summary: Cosmos SDK blockchain built around a decentralised exchange (AMM) for swapping tokens that arrive from other chains over IBC.
goodToKnow: App-chain: a blockchain built for one application, with its own validators.
Osmosis is the name of both the chain and the exchange running on it; OSMO is its native token.

detail.whatItIs: Osmosis is a Layer 1 blockchain built around one application: a decentralised exchange where users swap tokens and provide liquidity. Because it is connected through IBC to many Cosmos chains, and through bridges such as Axelar to Ethereum and others, it serves as a common place to trade tokens that originate on different chains. It launched in June 2021. The OSMO token is used for staking and governance, and holders vote on protocol upgrades and on which pools receive incentives.
detail.howItWorks: Osmosis runs on the Cosmos SDK with CometBFT consensus, so blocks are produced by a proof-of-stake validator set and are final as soon as they are committed. Trading happens through an automated market maker (AMM): instead of matching buyers and sellers, users trade against pools of two or more tokens, and a formula sets the price from the pool's balances. It offers several pool types, including concentrated liquidity, where providers choose a price range. Swap fees go to liquidity providers, while a separate taker fee goes to the protocol.

name: dYdX Chain
summary: Cosmos SDK blockchain dedicated to trading perpetual futures, with its order book run by the chain's validators.
goodToKnow: App-chain: a blockchain built for one application, with its own validators.
Earlier dYdX versions (v3 and before) ran on Ethereum and an Ethereum L2; dYdX Chain ("v4") is a separate network.

detail.whatItIs: dYdX Chain is a Layer 1 blockchain dedicated to one application: an exchange for perpetual futures, contracts that let traders bet on an asset's price with leverage and no expiry date. It launched in October 2023 as version 4 of dYdX, moving the exchange off Ethereum onto its own chain so that validators, not a company, run the matching. Traders post USDC as collateral. The DYDX token is used for staking and governance, and holders vote on new markets, parameters and upgrades.
detail.howItWorks: Each validator keeps an order book in memory, outside the chain's permanent record. Orders and cancellations travel between validators, and the validator proposing the next block matches them. Only the resulting trades and settlements are written into blocks, which CometBFT finalises in about a second. The other validators check that the proposed matches follow the rules before signing. Validators also supply oracle prices in each block, which the chain uses for margin checks and liquidations. Trading fees are distributed according to rules set by governance, including payments to stakers.

name: Polkadot
summary: Proof-of-stake network whose relay chain provides shared security to connected chains (parachains) that exchange messages via XCM.
goodToKnow: Polkadot Hub (the system chain for assets and smart contracts) enabled smart contracts on mainnet in January 2026.
Kusama is a separate, faster-moving sister network often used to try features before Polkadot.
DOT is used for staking, governance and fees.

detail.whatItIs: Polkadot is a proof-of-stake Layer 1 network designed to host many specialised blockchains at once. Its relay chain provides shared security, while connected chains, often called parachains or rollups, run their own applications and talk to each other with a message format called XCM. It was founded by Gavin Wood, a co-founder of Ethereum, and launched in 2020. DOT holders vote on upgrades and treasury spending through on-chain governance; no company has control over the network.
detail.howItWorks: Validators on the relay chain produce blocks about every six seconds and finalise them with a voting protocol called GRANDPA. Connected chains buy coretime, a share of the validators' processing time, and submit their blocks, which groups of validators re-check before they are included. Since November 2025, balances, staking and governance have lived on Polkadot Hub, a system chain, rather than on the relay chain itself. Since March 2026 a new issuance schedule caps the total DOT supply at 2.1 billion.

name: Monero
summary: Proof-of-work cryptocurrency designed for private payments, hiding the sender, receiver and amount of every transaction.
goodToKnow: Privacy is on by default: ring signatures hide the sender, stealth addresses hide the receiver and RingCT hides amounts, which is why on-chain tracing stops there.
Because of this, some exchanges have delisted XMR or restrict it in certain jurisdictions.
A planned upgrade (FCMP++) would replace ring signatures; as of November 2026 no mainnet date has been set.

detail.whatItIs: Monero is a cryptocurrency built for private payments. Every transaction hides who sent it, who received it and how much was moved, and this privacy is on by default rather than an option. It launched in April 2014 from the CryptoNote code base, without a premine, and is developed by an open community of contributors rather than a company. People use XMR as digital cash when they want financial privacy. Some exchanges have delisted it, for example Binance in February 2024.
detail.howItWorks: Monero uses proof of work with an algorithm called RandomX, designed to run well on ordinary computer processors, and a block is found about every two minutes. Each input is signed with a ring signature that mixes the real coin with 15 decoys, so observers cannot tell which one was spent. Stealth addresses give the receiver a fresh one-time address for every payment, and RingCT hides amounts while proving no coins were created from nothing. Since June 2022 a fixed tail emission of 0.6 XMR per block has continued indefinitely.

name: Lightning Network
summary: Payment network on top of Bitcoin that uses payment channels so users can send many small, fast payments off-chain.
goodToKnow: Only opening and closing a channel are Bitcoin transactions; payments in between are exchanged off-chain and routed through other nodes.
Receiving usually requires being online (or using a service that is), and a channel's capacity limits how much can move through it.
Lightning is not a rollup: it does not post transaction batches to Bitcoin.

detail.whatItIs: The Lightning Network is a payment network built on Bitcoin. Two people open a shared channel with one Bitcoin transaction, then pay each other many times, almost instantly and for tiny fees, settling the final balance on Bitcoin later. Payments can also hop across other people's channels to reach someone without a direct channel. Wallets, exchanges and shops use it for small, quick bitcoin payments. No company runs it: several teams write compatible node software following a shared set of specifications called BOLTs.
detail.howItWorks: Two parties lock bitcoin in a 2-of-2 multisignature output, which needs both of their signatures to spend. To pay, they sign a new commitment transaction that splits the funds differently and exchange secrets that revoke the previous one; if someone broadcasts an outdated state, the other party can claim all the funds during a waiting period. Payments across several channels use hashed time-locked contracts (HTLCs): each hop is paid only when the recipient reveals a secret, so either every hop completes or none does. Either party can close the channel on Bitcoin.

name: Arbitrum One
summary: Ethereum optimistic rollup that runs transactions off-chain and posts their data to Ethereum, with fraud proofs to settle disputes.
goodToKnow: Optimistic: results are assumed valid unless challenged, so native withdrawals to Ethereum take about a week.
"Arbitrum" also covers Arbitrum Nova (a separate chain) and the Orbit/Arbitrum chains framework used to launch other chains such as L3s.
Governed by the Arbitrum DAO (ARB token); the technology is developed mainly by Offchain Labs.

detail.whatItIs: Arbitrum One is a Layer 2 network for Ethereum: a separate chain where transactions are cheaper and faster, while Ethereum keeps the final record. It runs the same smart contracts as Ethereum, so DeFi apps, wallets and developer tools work on it with few changes. Its software, Nitro, was built mainly by Offchain Labs. The Arbitrum DAO, made up of ARB token holders, votes on upgrades and treasury spending, and an elected Security Council can act quickly in emergencies.
detail.howItWorks: A sequencer run by Offchain Labs orders transactions and confirms them in well under a second. It compresses them into batches and posts them to Ethereum, mostly as blobs. Validators then post claims about the resulting state. A wrong claim can be challenged: since February 2025 the BoLD protocol lets anyone take part in disputes, which narrow down to a single computation step that Ethereum executes. If no challenge succeeds within about 6.4 days, the claim is confirmed and withdrawals can complete. Stylus also allows contracts written in Rust and other languages compiled to WebAssembly.

name: OP Mainnet
summary: Ethereum optimistic rollup built with the OP Stack; it posts transaction data to Ethereum and uses fault proofs for withdrawals.
goodToKnow: "Optimism" is also the name of the foundation and of the Optimism Collective; OP Mainnet is the specific chain.
The OP Stack is open-source software used by other chains in the "Superchain"; Base, which launched on it, moved to its own stack in 2026.
Native withdrawals to Ethereum take about a week because of the challenge period.

detail.whatItIs: OP Mainnet is a Layer 2 network for Ethereum and the original chain built with the OP Stack, the open-source rollup software maintained by the Optimism Collective. Apps and wallets built for Ethereum work on it with little change, at lower fees. Governance is split between the Token House, where OP holders vote on upgrades and incentives, and the Citizens' House, which funds public goods through retroactive grants. The Optimism Foundation supports development and, as of November 2026, runs the chain's sequencer.
detail.howItWorks: The sequencer orders transactions into a block every two seconds and posts compressed batches to Ethereum, mostly as blobs. Proposers then publish output roots, short summaries of the chain's state, to Ethereum. Since June 2024 fault proofs are permissionless: anyone can propose or dispute an output root, and a dispute is settled by an interactive game that ends with Ethereum executing a single instruction. Since the Karst upgrade in July 2026, the main fault-proof program is Kona, written in Rust. A withdrawal can be finalised about seven days after its output root is proposed, if no dispute succeeds.

name: Base
summary: Ethereum optimistic rollup incubated by Coinbase; it runs transactions off-chain and settles them on Ethereum.
goodToKnow: Base launched on Optimism's OP Stack; with its Azul upgrade (mainnet 28 May 2026) it switched to its own base/base node software.
Base is operated by a company (Coinbase), which runs its sequencer; it is a separate network from the Coinbase exchange.
As of November 2026, Base combines TEE attestations and ZK proofs (since May 2026), so native withdrawals take about 1 to 5 days.

detail.whatItIs: Base is a Layer 2 network for Ethereum, developed and operated by Coinbase, the US crypto exchange company. It runs EVM smart contracts at low fees, and consumer apps, payment services and DeFi protocols are built on it. Fees are paid in ETH. Base launched in 2023 on Optimism's OP Stack. With the Azul upgrade on 28 May 2026 it moved to its own node software, base-reth-node and base-consensus, which replaced the OP Stack clients for anyone running a Base node.
detail.howItWorks: A single sequencer run by Coinbase orders transactions and produces a block every two seconds; a feature called Flashblocks streams partial blocks about every 200 milliseconds, so apps can show confirmations sooner. Transaction batches are posted to Ethereum as blobs. Since May 2026, claims about Base's state are checked with two kinds of evidence: attestations from trusted execution environments (TEEs, hardware enclaves that prove which code they ran) and zero-knowledge proofs. This replaces relying only on a week-long challenge window, so native withdrawals to Ethereum finish sooner.

name: ZKsync Era
summary: Ethereum zk-rollup (validity rollup) that proves its batches to Ethereum with zero-knowledge proofs; it is EVM-compatible.
goodToKnow: Validity proofs mean withdrawals do not need a week-long challenge period, though proof generation adds some delay.
Not to be confused with zkSync Lite, the earlier ZKsync rollup, which was deprecated in 2026.
Runs EraVM, its own virtual machine: Solidity compiles to EraVM bytecode, and standard EVM bytecode runs through an interpreter.

detail.whatItIs: ZKsync Era is a Layer 2 network for Ethereum built by Matter Labs. It is a zk-rollup: it runs transactions away from Ethereum and then proves to Ethereum, with a cryptographic proof, that they were processed correctly. Contracts written in Solidity can be deployed with little or no change, and every account can be a smart contract, which allows features such as paying fees in other tokens. ZK token holders vote on protocol upgrades, alongside a Security Council and a group called the Guardians.
detail.howItWorks: A sequencer operated by Matter Labs orders transactions into blocks and groups them into batches. For each batch, Era publishes the state changes to Ethereum, and a prover generates a validity proof: a short cryptographic proof that every transaction in the batch was executed correctly. A verifier contract on Ethereum checks the proof before accepting the new state, so no challenge window is needed, and withdrawals complete after that check. The Atlas upgrade of October 2025 introduced ZKsync OS and the Airbender prover as the new execution and proving design for chains built with the ZK Stack.

name: Starknet
summary: Ethereum validity rollup that uses STARK proofs; smart contracts are written in the Cairo language rather than for the EVM.
goodToKnow: Starknet is not EVM-compatible: Solidity contracts and Ethereum tooling need adaptation.
Every account on Starknet is a smart contract (native account abstraction).
Developed by StarkWare; STRK is the network token.

detail.whatItIs: Starknet is a Layer 2 network for Ethereum created by StarkWare. It is a validity rollup: it processes transactions away from Ethereum and proves their correctness to Ethereum with STARK proofs, a kind of zero-knowledge proof that needs no trusted setup. Contracts are written in Cairo, a language designed to be efficient to prove, so Ethereum contracts do not run on it directly. The Starknet Foundation supports the network, and STRK holders use the token to pay fees, stake and vote on upgrades.
detail.howItWorks: Since version 0.14.0 in September 2025, three sequencers take turns proposing blocks and run a consensus protocol to agree on them, so no single operator decides alone. Transactions run in the Cairo virtual machine, which records each step so it can be proven later. Since November 2025, StarkWare's S-two prover turns these records into STARK proofs. Proofs covering many blocks are combined and checked by a verifier contract on Ethereum, which then accepts the new state. Because every account is a smart contract, wallets can choose their own signature schemes, such as passkeys.

name: Linea
summary: Ethereum zk-rollup developed by Consensys that executes EVM transactions and proves them to Ethereum with zero-knowledge proofs.
goodToKnow: Gas is paid in ETH, not in the LINEA token.
Developed by Consensys, the company behind MetaMask.

detail.whatItIs: Linea is a Layer 2 network for Ethereum built by Consensys, the company behind MetaMask and Infura. It is a zk-rollup: a chain that runs transactions itself, then posts the data and a mathematical proof of correctness to Ethereum. Users and developers treat it much like Ethereum, with the same wallets, addresses and smart contract languages, but fees are lower. Gas is paid in ETH. The LINEA token, launched in September 2025, is not needed to use the network.
detail.howItWorks: A sequencer collects transactions and orders them into blocks about every two seconds. Linea's prover then takes batches of those blocks and produces a zero-knowledge proof: a short piece of cryptography showing that every step followed the EVM rules, without Ethereum having to re-run them. The proof and compressed transaction data are posted to Ethereum, where a verifier contract checks the proof. Once it passes, the new state is final, so withdrawals do not wait for a week-long challenge period as on optimistic rollups.

name: Scroll
summary: Ethereum zk-rollup that executes EVM transactions and proves them to Ethereum with zero-knowledge proofs.
goodToKnow: Aims for compatibility with Ethereum at the bytecode level, so most Ethereum contracts and tools work unchanged.
Gas is paid in ETH; SCR is the governance token.

detail.whatItIs: Scroll is a Layer 2 network for Ethereum. It is a zk-rollup: a chain that executes transactions away from Ethereum, then sends Ethereum the data plus a proof that the results are correct. It aims to behave like Ethereum at the bytecode level, so existing contracts, wallets and developer tools work with few or no changes. The project started in 2021 with open research on zkEVM circuits, and its mainnet opened in October 2023. Gas is paid in ETH; the SCR token is used for governance.
detail.howItWorks: A sequencer orders transactions into blocks, and batches of blocks are committed to Ethereum with their data in blobs. Provers then generate a validity proof for each batch. Since the Euclid upgrade in April 2025, Scroll's prover is built on OpenVM, a general-purpose zero-knowledge virtual machine, replacing its earlier hand-written halo2 circuits. A verifier contract on Ethereum checks each proof and finalises the batch. Users can also send transactions through a message queue contract on Ethereum, which the rollup has to process.

name: ApeChain
summary: Arbitrum Orbit L3 for the ApeCoin ecosystem that settles on Arbitrum One and uses APE as its gas token.
goodToKnow: "L3" has no single agreed definition; here it means a chain that settles on an L2 rather than directly on Ethereum.
Settlement layer (as of November 2026): Arbitrum One. Data is normally kept by a data availability committee (AnyTrust) rather than posted in full.
Built for the ApeCoin community; APE is the token, ApeChain is the network.

detail.whatItIs: ApeChain is a blockchain for the ApeCoin community, the ecosystem that grew around the Bored Ape Yacht Club NFT collection. It went live in October 2024 and hosts NFTs, games and other apps built around ApeCoin. It is a Layer 3: it settles on Arbitrum One, which in turn settles on Ethereum, so it inherits part of its security from both. Fees are paid in APE, the community's token, instead of ETH, which keeps the chain's economy tied to that token.
detail.howItWorks: ApeChain runs Arbitrum's Nitro software, configured with Arbitrum Orbit. A sequencer orders and executes transactions; summaries of the results are posted to Arbitrum One, where they can be challenged with fraud proofs during a dispute period. To keep costs low it uses AnyTrust: rather than posting all transaction data, a data availability committee stores it and signs a certificate promising to provide it. Full data goes to the parent chain only if not enough committee members sign. APE is bridged in to serve as the gas token.

name: Xai
summary: Gaming-focused Arbitrum Orbit L3 that settles on Arbitrum One and uses a data availability committee (AnyTrust).
goodToKnow: "L3" has no single agreed definition; here it means a chain that settles on an L2 rather than directly on Ethereum.
Settlement layer (as of November 2026): Arbitrum One.
Not related to xAI, the AI company; this Xai is a blockchain for games, with the XAI token.

detail.whatItIs: Xai is a blockchain for video games, launched in January 2024 by the games studio Ex Populus with support from Offchain Labs, the company behind Arbitrum. It aims to let games give players items and rewards they own on-chain, often through wallets the game manages so players need not handle crypto directly. It is a Layer 3 that settles on Arbitrum One. It is not related to xAI, the artificial intelligence company. XAI is its token, used for gas and node rewards.
detail.howItWorks: Xai runs Arbitrum Nitro in AnyTrust mode. A sequencer orders transactions, and a data availability committee keeps the transaction data and signs certificates instead of posting all of it to Arbitrum One, which lowers costs. State assertions are posted to Arbitrum One and can be challenged with fraud proofs. Xai adds Sentry nodes: anyone holding a Sentry Key licence can run software that checks the chain's assertions and raises an alarm if one looks wrong, earning esXAI, an escrowed form of the token, as a reward.

name: Uniswap
summary: Decentralised exchange protocol where users swap tokens against liquidity pools priced by an automated market maker (AMM).
goodToKnow: "Uniswap" can mean the on-chain protocol, the Uniswap Labs web app, or the UNI governance token.
Liquidity providers can lose value versus holding (impermanent loss) when prices move.
Deployed on Ethereum and many L2s and other chains; each deployment has separate pools.

detail.whatItIs: Uniswap is a set of smart contracts that let anyone swap one token for another, or deposit tokens into a pool and earn a share of trading fees, without an account and without a company holding the funds. It runs on Ethereum and many other networks. Uniswap Labs builds the main web and mobile apps, the Unichain network and much of the code, while UNI holders govern the protocol's fee settings and treasury. It is an application that runs on existing blockchains, not a chain of its own.
detail.howItWorks: Each pool holds two tokens, and an automated market maker formula sets the price from the pool's balances: in the original design their product stays constant, so buying one token makes it dearer. Since v3, liquidity providers can place funds within a chosen price range. Uniswap v4, launched in January 2025, keeps every pool in one contract and lets pool creators attach hooks, custom contracts that run before or after swaps. Since governance approved the UNIfication proposal in December 2025, part of the fees in some pools goes to the protocol and is used to burn UNI.

name: Aave
summary: Decentralised lending protocol where users deposit crypto to earn interest or borrow against collateral.
goodToKnow: Loans are over-collateralised; if collateral value falls too far, positions can be liquidated automatically.
Aave also issues its own stablecoin, GHO; AAVE is the governance token.
Aave v4, live on Ethereum since March 2026, shares liquidity through a central hub; v3 runs separate markets per network.

detail.whatItIs: Aave is a lending protocol: a set of smart contracts where people deposit crypto to earn interest and others borrow it by locking collateral worth more than the loan. There are no loan officers or credit checks; the rules are written in code. Aave also issues GHO, a stablecoin that borrowers mint. Holders of the AAVE token vote on new assets, risk limits and upgrades through the Aave DAO, and Aave Labs builds much of the software. It is an application that runs on Ethereum and several other networks.
detail.howItWorks: Each asset has a pool whose interest rate rises as more of it is borrowed, so lenders earn more when demand is high. A borrower's health factor compares collateral value, taken from Chainlink and other oracles, with the debt; when it drops below 1, anyone can repay part of the debt and receive collateral at a discount, which is called a liquidation. Aave v3 runs as separate markets on each network. Aave v4, live on Ethereum since March 2026, uses a hub-and-spoke design: hubs hold the liquidity, and spokes connect to them with their own collateral and risk rules.

sources.label: Aave blog: Aave V4 is live on Ethereum

name: Lido
summary: Liquid staking protocol for Ethereum: users stake ETH and receive stETH, a token that tracks their staked ETH and rewards.
goodToKnow: stETH is a claim on staked ETH; it can trade slightly away from 1 ETH on markets, and redemptions go through a withdrawal queue.
Staking is done by node operators chosen through Lido's governance; LDO is the governance token.
wstETH is a "wrapped" form of stETH whose balance does not change, used by many DeFi apps.

detail.whatItIs: Lido is a liquid staking protocol on Ethereum. Running your own Ethereum validator needs 32 ETH and technical skill; Lido lets anyone stake any amount of ETH and receive stETH, a token they can hold, sell or use as collateral while the ETH stays staked. Professional and community node operators run the validators. Holders of the LDO token govern the Lido DAO, which chooses operators and sets fees. Since Lido v3 went live in January 2026, organisations can also create their own staking vaults, called stVaults.
detail.howItWorks: Deposited ETH is assigned to node operators, who run validators but cannot take the funds: withdrawals can only go to a Lido contract. Each day an oracle committee reports validator balances, and the stETH balance in every wallet is adjusted, or rebased, to add rewards after a 10% fee split between operators and the DAO treasury. Withdrawal requests wait in a queue until enough ETH is available. An stVault is a separate contract with an operator chosen by its owner, who can mint stETH against the ETH staked in it, within limits set by Lido.

sources.label: Lido blog: Lido V3 is live

name: Sky (ex-MakerDAO)
summary: DeFi protocol issuing the USDS and DAI stablecoins against collateral; formerly MakerDAO, governed by SKY token holders.
goodToKnow: Formerly MakerDAO (rebranded to Sky in August 2024). DAI still exists and can be upgraded 1:1 to USDS; MKR upgrades to SKY at 24,000 SKY per MKR.
Since September 2025 late MKR upgrades carry a penalty that grows by one percentage point every three months.
Users mint stablecoins by locking collateral in vaults; under-collateralised vaults are liquidated. Vault prices come mainly from Chronicle oracles.

detail.whatItIs: Sky is the protocol formerly called MakerDAO, which created DAI, a decentralised stablecoin: a token designed to stay worth one US dollar. Since its rebrand in August 2024 it also issues USDS, and users can swap between DAI and USDS one-for-one. People use them for payments, trading and saving. Holders of the SKY token govern the protocol and set its rates, collateral and reserves. Sky also backs semi-independent projects called Stars, such as Spark, a lending protocol. It is an application on Ethereum.
detail.howItWorks: Users mint USDS or DAI by locking collateral in a vault, a contract that records their debt plus a stability fee, a form of interest. If collateral value, as reported by oracles such as Chronicle, falls below the required ratio, the collateral is auctioned to repay the debt. Part of the backing comes from protocol reserves, including USDC in a peg stability module that swaps it one-for-one, and tokenised real-world assets such as short-term government debt. Holders can deposit USDS in the Sky Savings Rate contract and receive sUSDS, which grows in value at a rate set by governance.

name: Curve
summary: Decentralised exchange whose AMM pools are designed for swapping similar-value assets, such as stablecoins, with low price impact.
goodToKnow: Its stableswap formula keeps prices tight while a pool is balanced; when one asset depegs, the pool fills up with it.
Curve also issues a stablecoin, crvUSD; CRV is the governance token.

detail.whatItIs: Curve is a decentralised exchange built mainly for swapping tokens that should trade at similar prices, such as different dollar stablecoins or different forms of staked ETH. Liquidity providers deposit tokens into pools and earn fees from swaps. Curve also runs pools for unrelated assets, a lending market called Llamalend and its own stablecoin, crvUSD. Holders who lock CRV as veCRV vote on governance and on how new CRV rewards are split between pools. It launched on Ethereum in 2020 and now runs on other networks too.
detail.howItWorks: Curve's stableswap formula behaves like a constant-sum pool, which trades one-for-one, while balances are close to equal, and shifts towards Uniswap's constant-product curve as a pool becomes unbalanced, so normal trades barely move the price. A later design, cryptoswap, concentrates liquidity around a moving internal price for volatile pairs. crvUSD is minted against collateral; its LLAMMA mechanism gradually converts a borrower's collateral into crvUSD as prices fall, and back as they recover, instead of one sudden liquidation. Locking CRV for longer, up to four years, gives more votes.

name: Jupiter
summary: Swap aggregator on Solana that routes trades across many exchanges to find a price; it also offers other trading products.
goodToKnow: An aggregator does not hold liquidity itself; it splits and routes orders through other Solana DEXs.
JUP is its governance token.

detail.whatItIs: Jupiter is a trading app on Solana, a Layer 1 blockchain built for fast, cheap transactions. Its core product is a swap aggregator: when a user wants to exchange one token for another, Jupiter compares prices across many decentralised exchanges (DEXs, exchanges run by smart contracts) and builds the trade for them. It also offers limit orders, recurring purchases and perpetual futures. A core team develops it, and JUP is its governance token. It is an application, not a chain, and it holds no liquidity of its own.
detail.howItWorks: A routing engine searches the liquidity pools of many Solana DEXs, such as Raydium, and can split one order across several pools and intermediate tokens to get a better rate. Jupiter also collects quotes from professional market makers through a request-for-quote system and picks the better result. The user's wallet then signs a single Solana transaction that performs every step at once: if the price moves beyond the user's slippage limit, the whole transaction fails and no tokens change hands. Since March 2026 developers reach this routing through one unified Swap API.

name: USDC (Circle)
summary: Dollar stablecoin issued by Circle, redeemable 1:1 for US dollars and backed by cash and short-term US government assets.
goodToKnow: Centrally issued: Circle can freeze USDC held at specific addresses.
Issued natively on many blockchains; "bridged" USDC on some chains is a different token from Circle-issued USDC.
Temporarily lost its peg in March 2023 when part of its reserves was held at Silicon Valley Bank.

detail.whatItIs: USDC is a digital dollar issued by Circle, a US company. Each token is meant to be worth one US dollar and can be redeemed for one by Circle's eligible customers. People use it to hold dollars on-chain, make payments, trade on exchanges and lend in DeFi apps. Circle issues it natively on many blockchains. Since 2023 Circle alone governs it, after the Centre consortium it formed with Coinbase was wound up. Circle also issues EURC, a separate euro token.
detail.howItWorks: Institutions send dollars to Circle through its Circle Mint service and receive newly minted USDC; when they redeem, Circle burns the tokens and returns dollars. Reserves are held as cash at banks and in the Circle Reserve Fund, a government money market fund managed by BlackRock, with monthly third-party attestations. In the US, the GENIUS Act, signed in July 2025, sets federal rules for payment stablecoins, and Circle received final approval for a national trust bank charter in July 2026. In the EU, Circle's French entity issues USDC under MiCA. CCTP moves USDC between chains by burning and minting.

name: USDT (Tether)
summary: Dollar stablecoin issued by Tether, intended to be redeemable 1:1 for US dollars and backed by Tether's reserves.
goodToKnow: Centrally issued: Tether can freeze USDT held at specific addresses.
USDT on BNB Chain is a Binance-issued token ("Binance-Peg") backed by USDT that Binance holds, not a Tether issuance.
Tether publishes the list of chains it issues on; versions elsewhere are bridged or third-party tokens.

detail.whatItIs: USDT, also called Tether, is a dollar stablecoin issued by Tether, a company now based in El Salvador. Each token is meant to be worth one US dollar. It is used on exchanges to move value between trades and, on chains such as TRON, for low-cost dollar transfers. Tether issues it natively on a list of chains it publishes. Tether also issues other tokens, including XAUT, backed by gold, and USAT, a separate dollar token designed for US rules.
detail.howItWorks: Verified customers send dollars to Tether, which mints USDT to them; redemption runs the other way, with Tether burning the tokens and paying out dollars, subject to minimums and checks. Tether says reserves are mostly US Treasury bills, with some gold, bitcoin and secured loans, and publishes quarterly attestations by the accounting firm BDO rather than full audits. USDT is issued outside the US and, as of November 2026, is not authorised under the EU's MiCA rules. USAT, launched in January 2026 and issued by Anchorage Digital Bank, is designed for the US GENIUS Act of July 2025.

name: Coinbase
summary: Centralised exchange where users buy, sell and hold crypto with traditional money; it also incubated the Base network.
goodToKnow: Centralised exchange (custodial): Coinbase holds users' keys, so funds there are an account balance, not self-custody.
Its self-custody app, Coinbase Wallet (called Base App from July 2025 to September 2026), is separate from exchange accounts.
Co-founded the Centre consortium with Circle that launched USDC in 2018.

detail.whatItIs: Coinbase is a US company, listed on Nasdaq since April 2021, that runs a centralised crypto exchange. People open an account, verify their identity, link a bank account or card, and then buy, sell and hold crypto. It also offers staking, derivatives trading and custody services for institutions. Coinbase incubated Base, an Ethereum layer 2 network, and runs its sequencer. Its self-custody app, renamed Base App in July 2025, went back to the name Coinbase Wallet in September 2026.
detail.howItWorks: Coinbase is custodial: it holds the private keys for customer crypto, mostly in offline cold storage, and its internal ledger records what each user owns. Trades on Coinbase Exchange are matched in a central limit order book, a list of buy and sell orders at set prices, on Coinbase's own servers, so they do not appear on a blockchain. Only deposits and withdrawals are on-chain transactions. Fiat on-ramps and off-ramps use bank transfers, cards and other payment rails. Revenue comes mainly from trading fees and spreads, plus staking, custody and a share of USDC reserve income.

sources.label: The Block: Base App renamed back to Coinbase Wallet (September 2026)

name: Kraken
summary: Centralised exchange where users buy, sell and hold crypto with traditional money; founded in 2011.
goodToKnow: Centralised exchange (custodial): Kraken holds users' keys, so funds there are an account balance, not self-custody.
Like other exchanges, it can freeze accounts or funds, for example at law-enforcement request.
Kraken also backs Ink, an Ethereum L2 network.

detail.whatItIs: Kraken is a centralised crypto exchange founded in 2011 in the US; its parent company is Payward. Users verify their identity, deposit traditional money or crypto, and trade, stake or withdraw. It also offers derivatives trading and services for institutions, and its subsidiary Kraken Financial has held a Wyoming special purpose depository institution charter, a state bank charter for digital assets, since 2020. Kraken backs Ink, an Ethereum layer 2 network built with the OP Stack.
detail.howItWorks: Kraken is custodial: it controls the private keys for deposited crypto, keeping most in offline cold storage, and tracks each user's balance in its own records. Orders are matched off-chain in central limit order books, so trades between users are not blockchain transactions; only deposits and withdrawals are. Fiat on-ramps and off-ramps use bank transfers and card payments, depending on the country. Since 2014 Kraken has published periodic proof-of-reserves checks, which use a Merkle tree so each user can confirm their balance was included. It earns money mainly from trading fees.

name: Chainlink
summary: Oracle network that brings off-chain data, such as asset prices, onto blockchains; it also offers cross-chain messaging (CCIP).
goodToKnow: An oracle is needed because smart contracts cannot fetch outside data themselves.
Price feeds are produced by independent node operators and aggregated on-chain.
LINK is the token used to pay node operators.

detail.whatItIs: Chainlink is a decentralised oracle network: a system that brings information from outside a blockchain, such as asset prices, onto it so that smart contracts can use it. Lending apps such as Aave rely on its price feeds to value collateral. It also offers CCIP, a protocol for sending tokens and messages between chains, plus verifiable randomness and automated contract calls. Its services run on Ethereum and many other chains. Chainlink Labs develops the software, while independent node operators run the network.
detail.howItWorks: Each price feed is served by a decentralised oracle network (DON), a group of independent node operators. Every node fetches prices from several data aggregators; using the Off-Chain Reporting protocol, the nodes agree on a median and co-sign one report, which a single transaction writes on-chain. A feed updates when the price moves past a set deviation threshold or when a heartbeat timer expires, and contracts simply read the latest answer. Node operators are paid in LINK, and LINK can also be staked as a backstop for service quality.

name: Pyth
summary: Oracle network that publishes price data contributed directly by trading firms and exchanges, for use on many blockchains.
goodToKnow: Prices are "pulled": an application (or user) posts a fresh signed price on-chain when it needs one, instead of the oracle pushing updates.
Prices are aggregated on Pythnet, Pyth's own appchain, then relayed to other chains.

detail.whatItIs: Pyth is an oracle network for financial market data. Instead of collecting prices from public websites, it receives them directly from first-party publishers: exchanges, trading firms and market makers that see the prices themselves. It offers feeds for crypto assets, equities, currencies and commodities, which lending, derivatives and trading apps on Solana, EVM chains and other networks read. PYTH token holders govern the protocol, for example by voting on fees, and Douro Labs is one of its main contributors.
detail.howItWorks: Each publisher submits its own price plus a confidence interval, a range expressing its uncertainty. Pythnet, Pyth's own appchain, combines these into one aggregate price and confidence interval, so a few outlying publishers cannot move the result much. Signed updates are served off-chain by a service called Hermes. When an app needs a price, it fetches the latest update and submits it to the Pyth contract on its chain in the same transaction, and the contract verifies it before use. Since August 2026 Hermes requires an API key, while the on-chain contracts stay permissionless.

name: The Graph
summary: Indexing protocol that organises blockchain data into queryable APIs ("subgraphs") that apps use to read on-chain data.
goodToKnow: It reads and indexes existing chain data; unlike an oracle, it does not bring outside data on-chain.
Indexers are paid in GRT for serving queries.

detail.whatItIs: The Graph is a decentralised indexing protocol. Reading history straight from a blockchain is slow, so apps and analysts use The Graph to query organised data, such as every swap in a Uniswap pool, through a GraphQL API. Developers define what to index in a subgraph, a small open-source specification, and publish it to the network, where independent indexers serve it for a fee. GRT is the token used to pay for queries and to stake. Since 2024 the protocol's contracts have run on Arbitrum One.
detail.howItWorks: A subgraph contains a manifest naming the contracts and events to watch, a GraphQL schema, and mapping code, usually written in AssemblyScript, that turns each event into stored records. Indexers run Graph Node software, which processes the chain block by block and keeps the results in a database. Apps send GraphQL queries through a gateway and pay query fees in GRT. Indexers stake GRT, which can be slashed for serving incorrect data, and delegators can add stake to them. Curators signal which subgraphs are worth indexing.

name: LayerZero
summary: Cross-chain messaging protocol that lets apps on different blockchains send messages and tokens to each other.
goodToKnow: Each app chooses which verifiers (DVNs) must confirm a message, so security depends on that app's configuration.
It is a messaging layer, not a single bridge; token bridges are built on top of it. ZRO is its token.

detail.whatItIs: LayerZero is a messaging protocol that lets smart contracts on different blockchains send data and instructions to each other. Developers use it to build cross-chain apps, such as tokens that exist on many chains at once under its OFT (Omnichain Fungible Token) standard, or token bridges such as Stargate. It is developed by LayerZero Labs, and ZRO is its governance token. It connects Ethereum and its Layer 2s with chains such as Solana, Aptos and BNB Chain. The protocol itself does not hold user funds.
detail.howItWorks: Each connected chain has an immutable Endpoint contract. An app sends a message to the Endpoint on the source chain. Independent verifiers called DVNs (decentralised verifier networks), chosen by the app, check that the message really happened and confirm it on the destination chain. Once the required DVNs agree, an Executor, a paid delivery service, passes the message to the receiving contract. Because each app picks its own DVNs and how many must agree, its security can range from a single verifier to several independent ones.

name: Wormhole
summary: Cross-chain messaging protocol in which a set of "Guardian" validators observe and sign messages passed between blockchains.
goodToKnow: Security relies on a fixed set of 19 Guardians; a message is valid once a two-thirds majority signs it.
Its bridge was exploited in February 2022 (about 120,000 ETH-equivalent minted); the loss was covered by Jump Crypto.
W is its token; Portal is a token bridge built on Wormhole.

detail.whatItIs: Wormhole is a cross-chain messaging protocol that lets apps on different blockchains, including Solana, Ethereum, Sui and Aptos, pass messages to each other. Developers build token bridges, such as Portal, and cross-chain token standards with it, including Native Token Transfers, which move a token between chains without creating wrapped copies. It was first built in 2020 by Jump Crypto to link Solana and Ethereum and is now developed by several contributors. W is its governance token.
detail.howItWorks: When an app emits a message through the Wormhole contract on one chain, each of the 19 Guardians, independent node operators, watches that chain and signs the message. Once at least 13 have signed, the signatures form a Verified Action Approval (VAA), which anyone can relay to the destination chain, where the Wormhole contract checks the signatures before the app acts. Security therefore depends on most Guardians being honest and keeping their keys safe. Some routes add extra checks, such as limits on how much value can move per day.

name: IBC
summary: Inter-Blockchain Communication: open protocol for chains to send tokens and data to each other, verified by on-chain light clients.
goodToKnow: Messages are verified by light clients of the other chain rather than a separate validator set; relayers only carry them.
Mainly used between Cosmos SDK chains, with work to connect other ecosystems.

detail.whatItIs: IBC, short for Inter-Blockchain Communication, is an open protocol that lets independent blockchains send tokens and arbitrary messages to each other. It is not a chain or a company product but a standard, written up as specifications called ICS, that chains build into their own software. It is used mostly between chains built with the Cosmos SDK, for example to move ATOM or USDC to a trading chain such as Osmosis. Token transfers use an application standard called ICS-20.
detail.howItWorks: Each chain runs a light client of the other: a small program that tracks the other chain's block headers and validator signatures. When chain A commits a packet to its state, an off-chain relayer carries the packet and a Merkle proof to chain B, whose light client checks that the packet really was committed. Relayers cannot forge messages; they only deliver them, and anyone can run one. For tokens, ICS-20 escrows the original on the source chain and mints a voucher on the destination, and a timeout refunds packets that are never delivered.

name: EigenLayer
summary: Ethereum restaking protocol: staked ETH and other assets can be reused to secure extra services in exchange for extra rewards.
goodToKnow: Restaking adds risk: the same stake can be slashed for misbehaviour on the additional services it secures.
Its developer, Eigen Labs, now presents EigenLayer as part of a wider "EigenCloud" platform; EIGEN is the token.
Services secured this way are called AVSs (Actively Validated Services); EigenDA is one example.

detail.whatItIs: EigenLayer is a restaking protocol on Ethereum. Restaking means reusing ETH that already secures Ethereum, or tokens such as stETH and EIGEN, as a deposit that also backs other services, called AVSs (Actively Validated Services), such as data availability layers, oracles or bridges. Stakers earn extra rewards in exchange for extra risk. Instead of recruiting their own validators, these services obtain security from EigenLayer's operators. It is built by Eigen Labs, which since 2025 presents it as the base of a wider EigenCloud platform.
detail.howItWorks: Stakers deposit liquid staking tokens into strategy contracts, or point their validators' withdrawal address to an EigenPod contract, then delegate to an operator who runs the software for one or more AVSs. Since slashing went live on mainnet in April 2025, each AVS defines operator sets with their own rules, and an operator allocates a fixed share of its delegated stake to each set, so a penalty in one set can only reach the stake allocated to it. Withdrawals pass through a waiting period before funds are released, so misbehaviour can still be punished.

sources.label: EigenCloud blog: slashing goes live on mainnet

name: EigenDA
summary: Data availability service secured by EigenLayer restaking, where rollups can post their transaction data instead of on Ethereum.
goodToKnow: Using external data availability lowers costs but means relying on EigenDA's operators rather than Ethereum to keep data retrievable.
It is a service built on EigenLayer, not a separate blockchain.

detail.whatItIs: EigenDA is a data availability service: a place where rollups, chains that rely on another chain for security, can publish their transaction data more cheaply than on Ethereum itself. It is an AVS built on EigenLayer, so the operators who store the data are backed by restaked ETH and EIGEN rather than by a blockchain of its own. Rollups using it still settle on Ethereum but rely on EigenDA's operators to keep data retrievable. Its second version, called Blazar, launched on mainnet in July 2025.
detail.howItWorks: A rollup sends a blob of data to a disperser, which erasure-codes it, splitting it into redundant chunks so that a sufficient subset can rebuild the whole, and computes KZG commitments, short cryptographic fingerprints that let each chunk be checked. Operators fetch their assigned chunks, check them against the commitments, store them and sign. The signatures are aggregated into a DA certificate, which the rollup posts to Ethereum instead of the full data. Verifier contracts on Ethereum check that operators holding enough stake signed it.

sources.label: EigenCloud blog: EigenDA V2 core architecture

name: Celestia
summary: Blockchain specialised in data availability: rollups and other chains publish their transaction data on it.
goodToKnow: It is its own chain dedicated to data availability, shown with tools here.
Celestia does not execute smart contracts for those chains; it orders and stores their data and lets light nodes check it by sampling.
TIA is its native token.

detail.whatItIs: Celestia is a blockchain specialised in data availability, meaning it guarantees that published data can be downloaded by anyone. Rollups and other chains post their transaction data to it as blobs, which costs less than posting to their settlement layer, while they execute transactions and settle elsewhere. Celestia does not run their smart contracts. Its mainnet launched in October 2023, and it is developed by Celestia Labs and other contributors. TIA is the native token, used to pay blob fees and for staking.
detail.howItWorks: Celestia is a proof-of-stake chain built with the Cosmos SDK and CometBFT consensus, secured by validators that stake TIA. The blob data in each block is arranged in a square and extended with two-dimensional erasure coding, so hiding even a small part would require withholding a large share. Light nodes then perform data availability sampling: they download a few random pieces and gain high confidence that the whole block is available without downloading it. Namespaced Merkle trees let each rollup fetch only its own data, and the Blobstream bridge relays Celestia commitments to Ethereum.

name: MetaMask
summary: Self-custody wallet by Consensys for Ethereum and EVM chains, with Solana and Bitcoin accounts since 2025; extension and mobile app.
goodToKnow: Self-custody: whoever has the Secret Recovery Phrase controls the funds; MetaMask cannot recover it.
MetaMask staff will never ask for your recovery phrase; requests for it are scams.

detail.whatItIs: MetaMask is a self-custody crypto wallet made by Consensys, available as a browser extension and a mobile app. It lets people hold tokens, sign transactions and connect to decentralised apps such as exchanges, lending protocols and NFT marketplaces. It started on Ethereum and works with EVM-compatible networks, the chains that run Ethereum-style smart contracts. Since its multichain accounts update in October 2025, each account also includes a Solana address, with Bitcoin addresses added as well.
detail.howItWorks: When a wallet is created, MetaMask generates a Secret Recovery Phrase of 12 words, from which all private keys are derived. The keys are encrypted with the user's password and stored on the device; MetaMask's servers never hold them. When a website requests a transaction, MetaMask shows the details, the user approves, and the wallet signs it locally before sending it to the network through a remote node, by default Infura. Hardware wallets such as Ledger can be connected so that signing happens on the device. Snaps, third-party plug-ins, add further chains and features.

name: Phantom
summary: Self-custody wallet app, originally for Solana and now supporting several other blockchains.
goodToKnow: Self-custody: whoever has the recovery phrase controls the funds; Phantom cannot recover it.

detail.whatItIs: Phantom is a self-custody wallet app, available as a browser extension and a mobile app, made by a US company of the same name. It started in 2021 as a wallet for Solana and later added other networks; as of November 2026 these include Ethereum, Base, Polygon, BNB Chain, HyperEVM and Bitcoin, while support for Sui ended in September 2026. People use it to hold tokens and NFTs, swap tokens inside the app and connect to Solana apps such as Jupiter.
detail.howItWorks: Phantom creates a recovery phrase on the user's device and derives a separate key pair for each supported chain from it. The keys are encrypted and stored locally, not on Phantom's servers. When an app asks for a signature, Phantom simulates the transaction, shows the expected balance changes and warns about known malicious sites before the user approves; it then signs locally and sends the transaction to the network. Users can also pair a Ledger hardware wallet, so the private key stays on that device and signing happens there.

name: Safe
summary: Smart contract wallet that can require several signatures (multisig) to approve a transaction; used to hold shared funds.
goodToKnow: A Safe is a smart contract account, so it exists separately on each chain where it is deployed.
Many DAOs and teams use it to control treasuries and protocol upgrades.

detail.whatItIs: Safe, formerly Gnosis Safe, is a smart contract wallet: an account that is itself a program on the blockchain rather than a single private key. Its standard setup is a multisig, which needs several owners to approve each transaction, for example three of five. DAOs, companies and protocol teams use it to hold shared funds and control contract upgrades, and individuals use it for extra security. It runs on Ethereum and many EVM networks, and Safe{Wallet} is its main interface.
detail.howItWorks: Each Safe stores a list of owners and a threshold, the number of approvals needed. Owners can be ordinary keys, hardware wallets, passkeys or other smart accounts. An owner proposes a transaction; others sign the same transaction hash off-chain, and once enough signatures are collected anyone can submit them to the Safe contract, which checks them and executes. Changing owners or the threshold needs the same approval. Optional modules add functions such as spending limits or recovery, and guards run checks before and after each transaction. Because a module can act without signatures, adding one needs owner approval.

name: ENS
summary: Ethereum Name Service: maps readable names such as alice.eth to wallet addresses and other data.
goodToKnow: .eth names are registered for a period and must be renewed, otherwise they can be registered by someone else.
ENS is not a DNS replacement, but some existing DNS domains can be linked to it.

detail.whatItIs: The Ethereum Name Service, ENS, gives readable names such as alice.eth to blockchain addresses, much as the web's DNS gives names to server addresses. Wallets that support it let people send funds to a name instead of a long hexadecimal address, and a name can also hold a website link, a profile picture or addresses on other chains. Names are tokens that can be transferred. The ENS DAO, made up of ENS token holders, governs the protocol, and ENS Labs develops it.
detail.howItWorks: A registry contract on Ethereum records who owns each name and which resolver, a contract holding the name's records, to ask. To look up alice.eth, an app finds the resolver and reads the address. .eth names are bought from a registrar contract for a yearly fee, with a grace period after expiry before they are released. ENSv2, live on Ethereum mainnet since 27 October 2026, lets each name act as its own registry for the names beneath it, with finer permissions. In February 2026 ENS Labs dropped a planned layer 2 and kept ENSv2 on Ethereum.

sources.label: ENS blog: ENSv2 is live on mainnet (October 2026)
ENS blog: ENS is staying on Ethereum (February 2026)

name: OpenSea
summary: Marketplace for buying and selling NFTs and other tokens across several blockchains.
goodToKnow: OpenSea is a company-run interface; the NFTs themselves live on-chain, in the user's wallet, not on OpenSea.
Listing on OpenSea typically means signing an off-chain order; read signature requests carefully, as phishing often abuses them.

detail.whatItIs: OpenSea is a marketplace website and app, run by a US company founded in 2017, where people buy, sell and make offers on NFTs, tokens that represent unique items such as art or collectibles. Since its OS2 relaunch in 2025 it also lets users trade ordinary tokens. It covers Ethereum and many other networks, and since August 2026 it again supports Solana NFTs. Creators can launch collections through OpenSea Studio, and anyone can browse without an account.
detail.howItWorks: OpenSea does not hold users' NFTs. On Ethereum and other EVM networks, a seller signs an off-chain order with their wallet, saying which item they will sell, at what price and until when, and approves Seaport, OpenSea's open-source exchange contract, to move that item. OpenSea stores the signed order and displays it. When a buyer accepts, their wallet sends a transaction to Seaport, which checks the signature and swaps payment and NFT in one step, also paying any fees. OpenSea's revenue comes mainly from a marketplace fee on sales.

sources.label: The Block: OpenSea adds Solana NFT trading (August 2026)

name: Etherscan
summary: Block explorer for Ethereum: a website to look up transactions, addresses, blocks and verified contract code.
goodToKnow: An explorer only displays public chain data; it does not hold funds and cannot reverse transactions.
Address labels and "verified" source code are Etherscan features (source is submitted by developers), not part of the chain itself.

detail.whatItIs: Etherscan is a block explorer: a website that turns raw Ethereum data into readable pages for each transaction, address, block and token. People use it to check whether a payment went through, see what a smart contract does, or follow funds. It is run by a private company, Etherscan, which also operates explorers for other chains, such as Arbiscan for Arbitrum One and BaseScan for Base. Developers use its API to fetch chain data and to verify contract source code.
detail.howItWorks: Etherscan runs its own nodes, reads every new block and stores the data in its own databases, adding indexes so that an address's full history can be found quickly. Developers can upload a contract's source code; Etherscan compiles it and checks that the result matches the code deployed on-chain, then marks it as verified. Since 2025 its API V2 uses one key across many chains, with free and paid plans; as of November 2026, some chains require a paid plan. Revenue comes from API subscriptions and advertising, while the website itself is free to browse.

sources.label: Etherscan: changes in free API tier coverage

name: Alchemy
summary: Company providing node access (RPC) and developer APIs so apps can read from and send transactions to blockchains.
goodToKnow: Many apps rely on hosted providers like Alchemy instead of running their own nodes, which concentrates infrastructure in a few companies.

detail.whatItIs: Alchemy is a private company that sells blockchain infrastructure to developers. Instead of running their own nodes, which takes storage, bandwidth and maintenance, apps send requests to Alchemy's servers to read chain data and submit transactions. It supports Ethereum, many Layer 2 networks, Solana and other chains. Wallets, exchanges and DeFi apps use it behind the scenes, so end users rarely see it. It also offers tools for smart wallets, which use account abstraction so users can sign in without managing a seed phrase.
detail.howItWorks: Alchemy runs large fleets of blockchain nodes and puts load balancing and caching in front of them. Apps call a standard JSON-RPC endpoint, the same interface a node exposes, using an API key. In addition, Alchemy indexes chain data into its own databases to answer questions a plain node cannot answer quickly, such as all tokens or NFTs held by an address, and it can send webhooks when something happens on-chain. Customers pay by metered usage, with a free tier for small projects. Because responses come from Alchemy, apps trust it to return correct data.

name: Flashbots
summary: Research and development group behind MEV-Boost and Flashbots Protect, software that shapes how Ethereum blocks are built.
goodToKnow: MEV-Boost runs proposer-builder separation outside the protocol: validators accept full blocks from builders, through relays.
Flashbots Protect is an RPC endpoint that keeps transactions out of the public mempool, to reduce front-running.

detail.whatItIs: Flashbots is a research and development organisation that works on MEV, maximal extractable value: the profit available from choosing which transactions go into a block and in what order. It publishes open-source software that many Ethereum validators and traders use. MEV-Boost connects validators to specialised block builders. Flashbots Protect lets users send transactions privately. BuilderNet, launched in December 2024, is a block builder run jointly by several operators. Flashbots is not a blockchain; it is infrastructure that sits beside Ethereum.
detail.howItWorks: With MEV-Boost, a validator due to propose a block does not build it. Builders assemble full blocks and send bids to relays, which check the blocks and forward the highest bid. The validator signs the block header without seeing its contents, then the relay releases the full block, so neither side can cheat the other. Protect sends transactions straight to builders and can refund users part of the value they create. As of November 2026, Ethereum's planned Glamsterdam upgrade would build proposer-builder separation into the protocol itself (ePBS), without trusted relays; its mainnet date was not yet set.

name: OpenZeppelin
summary: Security company known for its open-source library of audited smart contract building blocks (ERC-20, ERC-721, access control).
goodToKnow: Using OpenZeppelin Contracts reduces risk but does not make a project secure by itself; custom code still needs review.
OpenZeppelin also performs smart contract security audits.

detail.whatItIs: OpenZeppelin is a software security company. Developers know it mainly for OpenZeppelin Contracts, a free, open-source library of reusable smart contract building blocks: token standards such as ERC-20 and ERC-721, access control, upgradeable proxies and governance modules. Instead of writing these from scratch, teams import reviewed code. The company earns money from security audits and related services. It announced in 2025 that its hosted Defender platform would close on 1 July 2026, with its relayer and monitoring tools released as open source instead.
detail.howItWorks: The Contracts library is written in Solidity, and versions exist for other languages such as Cairo for Starknet. A developer installs it with a package manager and inherits from its contracts, for example extending ERC20 and adding a custom minting rule. Each release is reviewed and tested, follows Ethereum standards closely and uses semantic versioning, so breaking changes only come in major versions such as 5.0. Upgradeable variants work with proxy contracts, which keep a fixed address while pointing to new logic. Audits are manual reviews by security researchers, who report vulnerabilities to the client before deployment.

name: OP Stack
summary: Open-source software kit from Optimism for building Ethereum rollups; OP Mainnet, Unichain and Ink are built with it.
goodToKnow: A framework, not a chain: each OP Stack chain runs separately, with its own operator and settings, but shares the same core code.
As of November 2026 it is used by OP Mainnet, Unichain, Ink, World Chain, Soneium, Celo and (modified) Mantle. Base launched on it, then moved to its own node software in 2026.
OP Stack chains are optimistic rollups with fault proofs by default, but some, such as Mantle, swap in ZK validity proofs.

detail.whatItIs: The OP Stack is open-source software, published by the Optimism Collective and OP Labs, for building Layer 2 rollups that settle on Ethereum. A team that wants its own chain can start from this shared code instead of writing a rollup from scratch. OP Mainnet is its reference chain, and many others, including Unichain, Ink and a modified Mantle, run on it. Chains that adopt shared standards and governance can join the Superchain, Optimism's network of cooperating OP Stack chains.
detail.howItWorks: A team gets the core parts: an execution client (op-geth or op-reth) that runs EVM transactions, op-node, which rebuilds the chain from data posted to Ethereum, a batcher that posts transaction data, and a proposer that publishes state roots. Fault-proof contracts let anyone challenge a wrong state root on Ethereum. The team still chooses its gas settings, block time, where data is stored, and whether to keep fault proofs or swap in ZK proofs. It must run the sequencer itself or pay a rollup-as-a-service provider to do so.

name: Arbitrum Orbit
summary: Offchain Labs' kit for launching custom chains on Arbitrum's Nitro software; ApeChain and Xai are built with it.
goodToKnow: As of November 2026 the official docs call these "Arbitrum chains"; "Orbit" is the earlier name, still widely used.
A chain can settle on Ethereum or on an Arbitrum L2 (making it an L3), use a custom gas token, and post data in full (Rollup) or to a committee (AnyTrust).
Degen Chain was also built with it until it shut down on 31 August 2026.

detail.whatItIs: Arbitrum Orbit is the programme and software kit from Offchain Labs for launching custom chains based on Arbitrum's technology; as of November 2026 the official docs call them Arbitrum chains. A team gets the same Nitro software that runs Arbitrum One, but on its own separate chain. Chains can settle on Ethereum as Layer 2s, or on an Arbitrum Layer 2 as Layer 3s. Games, NFT communities and companies have used it to launch chains such as ApeChain and Xai.
detail.howItWorks: A team gets Nitro: node software that runs EVM transactions, plus a sequencer, a batch poster and a validator that posts assertions about the chain's state. Disputes are settled by interactive fraud proofs on the parent chain, with BoLD as the newer dispute protocol. The team still chooses its parent chain, gas token, Rollup or AnyTrust data mode, and who may act as validator. It must run or outsource the sequencer and nodes. Chains that settle outside Arbitrum One and Nova share part of their revenue with the Arbitrum DAO.

sources.label: Arbitrum docs: launch an Arbitrum chain

name: ZK Stack
summary: Matter Labs' open-source kit for building chains proven with zero-knowledge proofs; ZKsync Era is built with it.
goodToKnow: As of November 2026, chains built with it include ZKsync Era and Lens Chain. Abstract, also built with it, announced it will shut down on 15 December 2026.
A chain can be a rollup (data posted to Ethereum) or a validium (data kept elsewhere), which changes what users have to trust.
Its components include ZKsync OS and the Airbender prover; chains built with it are sometimes called the Elastic Network.
