detail.whatItIs: The ZK Stack is open-source software from Matter Labs for launching blockchains whose correctness is proven with zero-knowledge proofs. It is the code behind ZKsync Era, and other teams use it to create their own chains, such as Lens Chain. Chains built with it can connect to each other through shared contracts on Ethereum, a group sometimes called the Elastic Network. It is aimed at teams that want their own chain, for example with custom access rules or privacy, without designing a proof system themselves.
detail.howItWorks: A team gets a sequencer, ZKsync OS as the execution layer, the Airbender prover that produces zero-knowledge proofs of each batch, and contracts on Ethereum that verify those proofs and hold bridged assets. Because Ethereum checks a proof rather than waiting for challenges, withdrawals do not need a long challenge period. The team still chooses its gas token, whether data goes to Ethereum as a rollup or is kept elsewhere as a validium, and who may use the chain. It must run the sequencer and provers itself or pay someone to.

name: Cosmos SDK
summary: Open-source Go framework for building application-specific blockchains; Cosmos Hub, Osmosis and dYdX Chain use it.
goodToKnow: A toolkit, not a network: each chain built with it has its own validators and token, and can connect to others through IBC.
As of November 2026, chains built with it include Cosmos Hub, Osmosis, dYdX Chain, Celestia and Axelar. It is usually paired with CometBFT (formerly Tendermint) consensus.
"Cosmos" can mean this SDK, the Cosmos Hub chain, or the wider ecosystem of IBC-connected chains.

detail.whatItIs: The Cosmos SDK is an open-source framework, written in Go, for building application-specific blockchains: chains designed for one main use, such as an exchange or a data network. Each chain built with it is fully independent, with its own validators, token and rules. It was first used in production when the Cosmos Hub launched in 2019. As of November 2026 it is maintained by Cosmos Labs, which also looks after CometBFT, the IBC protocol and Cosmos EVM, a module that adds Ethereum compatibility.
detail.howItWorks: A team gets ready-made modules for accounts, tokens, staking, governance and IBC, and writes its own modules for its application logic. The SDK connects to a consensus engine, usually CometBFT, through an interface called ABCI. CometBFT is a Byzantine fault tolerant protocol: validators vote in rounds, and a block is final once validators holding more than two-thirds of the voting power sign it, so confirmed blocks are never reorganised. The team still has to launch a token, recruit validators, set staking and fee rules, and run infrastructure such as RPC nodes.

sources.label: Cosmos blog: the Cosmos Stack roadmap for 2026

name: Polkadot SDK
summary: Parity's open-source Rust toolkit (formerly Substrate) for building blockchains; Polkadot itself and Avail use it.
goodToKnow: Brings Substrate, FRAME, Cumulus and the Polkadot node into one repository; chains can run on their own or connect to Polkadot.
As of November 2026, chains built with it include Polkadot, Kusama, Polkadot parachains and standalone chains such as Avail.
Building with the SDK does not by itself make a chain part of Polkadot or secured by it.

detail.whatItIs: The Polkadot SDK is an open-source Rust toolkit, mainly developed by Parity Technologies, for building blockchains. It combines Substrate, the base framework; FRAME, a library of ready-made modules called pallets; Cumulus, which lets a chain connect to Polkadot; and the Polkadot node itself. Teams use it to build either standalone chains or chains that rely on Polkadot for security. The Polkadot and Kusama networks are built with it, as is Avail, which runs independently of Polkadot.
detail.howItWorks: A team writes its chain's rules, called the runtime, by combining FRAME pallets for balances, staking or governance with its own logic. The runtime is compiled to WebAssembly and stored on-chain, so the chain can upgrade itself through a transaction instead of a hard fork. For a standalone chain the team picks consensus, often BABE or Aura for block production and GRANDPA for finality, and must run its own validators. To connect to Polkadot instead, it buys coretime and lets Polkadot's validators check its blocks.

sources.label: Polkadot docs: intro to Polkadot SDK

name: Aptos
summary: Proof-of-stake layer-1 blockchain that runs Move smart contracts and executes transactions in parallel (Block-STM).
goodToKnow: Started by former members of Meta's Diem (Libra) project, as was Sui; both use Move, but their designs differ.
Block-STM runs transactions in parallel optimistically and re-executes those that conflict, so developers do not declare dependencies.
APT is the native token, used for fees and staking.

detail.whatItIs: Aptos is a public proof-of-stake blockchain for smart contracts written in Move, a programming language that treats digital assets as resources that cannot be copied or accidentally destroyed. It hosts trading, stablecoin and payment apps. Aptos Labs, founded in 2021 by former members of Meta's Diem project, builds the core software, and the Aptos Foundation supports the ecosystem. Its mainnet launched in October 2022. Validators run the network, and APT holders can stake with them. It is a Layer 1, settling transactions on its own chain.
detail.howItWorks: Validators first share transactions with each other in batches, a design called Quorum Store, so consensus only has to order short references to those batches. They then agree on block order with a Byzantine fault tolerant (BFT) protocol, one that keeps working while less than a third of stake misbehaves. This protocol, originally AptosBFT, has been upgraded step by step since June 2025 toward a newer design called Raptr. Block-STM then executes each block in parallel, detects transactions that read data another one changed, and re-runs only those, so the result matches running them one by one.

sources.label: Aptos Foundation: Baby Raptr on mainnet

name: Sui
summary: Proof-of-stake layer-1 blockchain built around objects and the Move language, processing unrelated transactions in parallel.
goodToKnow: Assets are objects with owners; transactions that touch only their own objects can be processed in parallel with others.
Developed by Mysten Labs, founded by former Meta Diem engineers; its Move dialect differs from Aptos's.
SUI is the native token, used for gas and staking; validators reach consensus with Mysticeti, a DAG-based protocol (as of November 2026).

detail.whatItIs: Sui is a public proof-of-stake blockchain for smart contracts written in Sui Move, a version of the Move language. Instead of account balances, it stores everything as objects, each with an ID and an owner, such as a coin, an NFT or a game item. People use it for trading, payments, games and stablecoins. Mysten Labs builds the core software, and the Sui Foundation supports the ecosystem. Independent validators run the network, and SUI holders can stake with them. It is a Layer 1.
detail.howItWorks: Each transaction lists the objects it uses. An object owned by one address cannot be touched by anyone else, so transactions on different objects can run at the same time. Validators order transactions with Mysticeti: each validator keeps proposing blocks that reference other validators' blocks, building a shared graph, and parts of it are committed without waiting on a single leader. Since Mysticeti v2, announced in November 2025, validators check transactions inside consensus instead of in a separate earlier step. The validator set and stake weights can change at each epoch, which lasts about one day.

name: TRON
summary: Delegated proof-of-stake layer-1 blockchain with an EVM-compatible virtual machine (TVM); Tether issues USDT on it.
goodToKnow: 27 elected "Super Representatives" produce blocks; TRX holders vote for them by staking.
The TVM runs Solidity contracts, but TRON addresses (starting with T), its fee model (energy and bandwidth) and tooling differ from Ethereum's.
Founded by Justin Sun; TRX is the native token.

detail.whatItIs: TRON is a public blockchain that launched its own mainnet in 2018. It is often used to send stablecoins such as USDT, because transfers are fast and cheap, and it also hosts lending, trading and gaming apps. Its native token, TRX, is staked to vote and to obtain the resources that pay for transactions. Its virtual machine runs smart contracts written in Solidity, the language used on Ethereum. The TRON DAO, which grew out of the TRON Foundation, supports the network. It is a Layer 1.
detail.howItWorks: TRON uses delegated proof of stake. TRX holders stake tokens to receive votes, and the 27 candidates with the most votes become Super Representatives, with the ranking recounted every six hours. They take turns producing a block about every three seconds. Instead of paying gas on every transaction, accounts use two resources: bandwidth, which covers the size of a transaction, and energy, which covers running contract code. Staking TRX gives an account an allowance of both that refills over a day; anything beyond that is paid by burning TRX.

name: TON
summary: Proof-of-stake layer-1 blockchain first designed by Telegram, now run by an independent community, with its own virtual machine.
goodToKnow: Telegram dropped the project in 2020 after a US SEC lawsuit; the open-source network continued as "The Open Network", supported by the TON Foundation.
Its virtual machine (TVM) is neither the EVM nor TRON's TVM: contracts are written in languages like FunC, Tolk or Tact and talk by asynchronous messages.
Telegram's apps connect to TON (e.g. wallets and Mini Apps), but Telegram does not run the network.

detail.whatItIs: TON, short for The Open Network, is a public proof-of-stake blockchain whose native coin is Toncoin. People use it for payments, stablecoin transfers, tokens, NFTs and Telegram Mini Apps, small apps that open inside the Telegram messenger. Telegram designed it in 2018 and abandoned it in 2020; open-source developers kept it running, and today the TON Foundation and the TON Core development team support it. Independent validators run the network, and Toncoin holders can stake with them through nominator pools. It is a Layer 1.
detail.howItWorks: TON is built as a set of chains. A masterchain holds the validator list and the latest state of every other chain. Workchains hold accounts and contracts, and split into shardchains when busy, then merge again when activity drops. Validators stake Toncoin and agree on blocks with Catchain, a Byzantine fault tolerant protocol. Since Catchain 2.0 reached mainnet in April 2026, blocks arrive about every 400 milliseconds and are usually final in about one second. Contracts never call each other directly: they send messages that are processed in later blocks.

name: NEAR
summary: Sharded proof-of-stake layer-1 blockchain whose smart contracts compile to WebAssembly, usually written in Rust or JavaScript.
goodToKnow: Nightshade sharding splits the network into shards that process transactions in parallel; accounts have readable names like alice.near.
Not EVM-native: Ethereum tools do not work directly; an EVM environment (Aurora) runs as a separate project on top of NEAR.
Chain Signatures let NEAR accounts sign transactions on other blockchains (as of November 2026).

detail.whatItIs: NEAR is a public proof-of-stake blockchain designed for apps that need low fees and simple accounts. Accounts have readable names, like alice.near, and can hold several keys with different permissions, which makes wallets easier to use. NEAR has added features for working across chains, such as Chain Signatures and NEAR Intents, where a user states the outcome they want and independent solvers compete to deliver it. The NEAR Foundation, a Swiss non-profit, supports the ecosystem, and independent validators run the network. It is a Layer 1.
detail.howItWorks: NEAR uses Nightshade sharding: each block is made of chunks, one per shard, and each shard handles a slice of accounts. Since Nightshade 2.0 in August 2024, validators can check a chunk without storing that shard's data, using a proof of the state it touches; this is called stateless validation. Doomslug, the block production protocol, makes a block practically irreversible after one round and fully final after a second. Since May 2025, a block arrives about every 600 milliseconds and is typically final in about 1.2 seconds. Contracts compile to WebAssembly and pay gas in NEAR tokens.

name: Hyperliquid
summary: Layer-1 blockchain built for trading: on-chain order books (HyperCore) plus an EVM smart-contract layer (HyperEVM).
goodToKnow: HyperCore and HyperEVM are two parts of one chain, both secured by HyperBFT, a HotStuff-inspired proof-of-stake consensus (as of November 2026).
It has a much smaller validator set than Ethereum, which helps speed but concentrates control in fewer hands.
HYPE is the native token, used for gas and staking. Hyperliquid is its own L1, not an Ethereum L2 or rollup.

detail.whatItIs: Hyperliquid is a blockchain built mainly for trading. Its core is an exchange for spot tokens and perpetual futures, contracts that track an asset's price with no expiry date, where every order, cancellation and liquidation is recorded on-chain instead of in a company's private database. Traders usually deposit USDC as collateral. A second part, HyperEVM, runs Ethereum-style smart contracts that can use the exchange's data. Hyperliquid Labs develops the software, and a set of validators runs the chain. It is a Layer 1, not an Ethereum Layer 2.
detail.howItWorks: HyperBFT, a proof-of-stake protocol derived from HotStuff, orders a single sequence of blocks for both parts of the chain. HyperCore holds the order books, margin accounts and oracle prices, and matches orders as part of block execution. HyperEVM contracts read HyperCore state through precompiled contracts and send it actions through a system contract called CoreWriter. HyperEVM mixes small, frequent blocks with larger, rarer ones for heavy contracts. As of November 2026, under HIP-3, a builder who stakes 500,000 HYPE can run a separate perpetuals market with its own oracle, and validators can slash that stake for misconduct.

name: Polygon PoS
summary: Proof-of-stake EVM chain that regularly checkpoints its state to Ethereum; often called a sidechain rather than a rollup.
goodToKnow: Its own validators secure it: Ethereum stores checkpoints but does not verify each transaction, so it does not inherit Ethereum's security like a rollup.
POL replaced MATIC as the gas and staking token in September 2024; most MATIC has since been migrated to POL.
Hard forks in 2025–2026 (e.g. Heimdall v2, Rio, Giugliano) aimed at faster finality; as of November 2026 it remains a PoS chain, not a rollup.

detail.whatItIs: Polygon PoS is an EVM-compatible blockchain that runs alongside Ethereum. Its fees are low, so it is used for payments, stablecoin transfers, games and apps such as the prediction market Polymarket, and Ethereum wallets and tools work with it unchanged. It is often called a sidechain: it has its own validators and records periodic checkpoints on Ethereum, but Ethereum does not check its transactions. Polygon Labs develops it, and its gas and staking token has been POL since September 2024.
detail.howItWorks: The chain has two layers. Validators stake POL in contracts on Ethereum. Heimdall, the consensus layer, tracks that stake, chooses block producers and regularly submits a checkpoint to Ethereum: a hash summarising recent blocks, signed by validators holding more than two-thirds of the stake. Bor, the execution layer, is based on Ethereum's Geth client and produces a block about every two seconds. Heimdall v2, live since July 2025, cut finality from over a minute to a few seconds, and the Giugliano hard fork of April 2026 shortened it by about two more seconds.

sources.label: Polygon blog: MATIC to POL migration

name: Zcash
summary: Proof-of-work cryptocurrency that adds optional private (shielded) transactions using zero-knowledge proofs (zk-SNARKs).
goodToKnow: Privacy is optional: transparent addresses work like Bitcoin's; only shielded transactions hide sender, receiver and amount.
Launched in 2016 from a fork of Bitcoin's code; ZEC is the native coin.
Crosslink, a proposed hybrid of proof of work and proof of stake, is being tested but is not active on mainnet as of November 2026.

detail.whatItIs: Zcash is a cryptocurrency that combines a Bitcoin-like public ledger with an optional private mode. Users can send ZEC between transparent addresses, visible to everyone, or move it into a shielded pool where transactions hide sender, receiver and amount. Shielded users can share a viewing key so that an auditor or tax authority can see their transactions without being able to spend the funds. It launched in October 2016, and development is funded partly by a share of block rewards set through community governance.
detail.howItWorks: Zcash uses proof of work with the Equihash algorithm and produces a block about every 75 seconds. Shielded transactions carry zk-SNARKs, zero-knowledge proofs showing that a payment is valid, with no double spend and balanced amounts, without revealing its details. Since the NU5 upgrade in May 2022, the newest shielded pool, Orchard, uses Halo 2 proofs that need no trusted setup ceremony. Unified addresses bundle a user's transparent and shielded receivers into one address, so the sender's wallet can pick the shielded option whenever it supports it.

name: Stacks
summary: Smart-contract network anchored to Bitcoin through Proof of Transfer; it calls itself a Bitcoin L2, a label some dispute.
goodToKnow: Proof of Transfer: miners spend BTC to win Stacks blocks, and STX holders who lock ("stack") tokens can earn that BTC; blocks are anchored in Bitcoin transactions.
Critics call it a separate chain rather than a true L2: it has its own token (STX) and consensus, and Bitcoin does not verify its transactions.
Contracts use the Clarity language; sBTC is a 1:1 BTC-backed asset on Stacks, managed by a set of signers.

detail.whatItIs: Stacks is a blockchain that adds smart contracts and apps to Bitcoin without changing Bitcoin itself. It records its progress in Bitcoin transactions, and Stacks says that rewriting its history would require rewriting Bitcoin's too. It has its own token, STX, and contracts written in Clarity, a language whose source code is stored on-chain and whose effects can be analysed before it runs. Through sBTC, users bring BTC onto Stacks for lending and trading. It began as Blockstack in 2013, and the Stacks Foundation supports the ecosystem.
detail.howItWorks: In Proof of Transfer, miners bid BTC in Bitcoin transactions for the right to lead a Stacks tenure, and the winner is drawn at random, weighted by bid size. That BTC goes to STX holders who have locked, or stacked, their tokens. Since the Nakamoto upgrade in October 2024, the tenure leader produces Stacks blocks every few seconds, and signers, chosen from stackers, must approve each block. The same signers manage sBTC: deposits lock BTC at a Bitcoin address they control, and a withdrawal needs approval from a large majority of them.

name: Rootstock
summary: EVM-compatible sidechain merge-mined with Bitcoin, using a two-way peg (PowPeg) that locks BTC to issue RBTC.
goodToKnow: Often marketed as a "Bitcoin L2", but its own docs call it a sidechain: it has its own consensus, and the peg relies on a multisig of approved signers.
Bitcoin miners can mine it at the same time (merged mining), so it reuses Bitcoin's hash power without extra energy.
RBTC, pegged 1:1 to BTC, pays fees; PowPeg keys sit in hardware devices (PowHSMs) that sign only with enough proof of work behind them.

detail.whatItIs: Rootstock is a blockchain linked to Bitcoin that runs smart contracts compatible with Ethereum's, so Solidity code and Ethereum wallets work on it. Users move BTC onto it, where it becomes RBTC, and use it in lending, trading and payment apps while keeping exposure to bitcoin. It launched in January 2018. The company RootstockLabs develops much of its software, and Bitcoin mining pools help secure it. Its own documentation describes it as a sidechain: a separate chain connected to Bitcoin by a two-way bridge.
detail.howItWorks: Rootstock blocks are produced by merged mining: a Bitcoin mining pool includes a reference to a Rootstock block in the work it does for Bitcoin, so the same hashing secures both chains. A new block arrives roughly every 30 seconds. The PowPeg bridge moves BTC: a user sends BTC to a Bitcoin address controlled by a federation of functionaries, and the Bridge contract on Rootstock releases the same amount of RBTC. Pegging out reverses this, and the functionaries' PowHSM devices sign the Bitcoin release only after enough Rootstock blocks confirm the request.

name: Unichain
summary: Ethereum optimistic rollup on the OP Stack, launched by Uniswap Labs for DeFi and fast trading.
goodToKnow: The Uniswap protocol runs on many chains; Unichain is a separate network that Uniswap Labs launched (mainnet February 2025).
Like other OP Stack chains, withdrawals to Ethereum rely on fault proofs and a challenge period (as of November 2026).
Blocks are built inside a TEE and streamed as sub-second "Flashblocks" preconfirmations; final settlement still happens on Ethereum.

detail.whatItIs: Unichain is a Layer 2 network for Ethereum launched by Uniswap Labs, the company that develops the Uniswap trading protocol; its mainnet has been live since February 2025. It is built for decentralised finance: trading, lending and moving tokens with fast confirmation and low fees. It is an optimistic rollup, meaning results posted to Ethereum are assumed correct unless someone proves otherwise. It belongs to Optimism's Superchain, a group of OP Stack chains that share standards and upgrades.
detail.howItWorks: Unichain produces a block every second, and within each block it streams partial blocks called Flashblocks about every 200 milliseconds, giving apps a near-instant preconfirmation. Block building runs inside a trusted execution environment (TEE), a sealed hardware area meant to stop the builder from secretly reordering transactions for profit. Transaction batches are posted to Ethereum. Anyone can challenge a wrong result with a fault proof during a challenge period of about seven days, which is why standard withdrawals to Ethereum take that long.

name: Mantle
summary: Ethereum rollup on a modified OP Stack that uses ZK validity proofs (OP Succinct) and posts its data to Ethereum.
goodToKnow: Started as an optimistic rollup; since September 2025 OP Succinct ZK proofs (SP1) validate its state, shortening withdrawals from about 7 days.
Data availability: Mantle used EigenDA from 2025, then moved to Ethereum blobs; its April 2026 Arsia upgrade removed EigenDA (as of November 2026).
MNT is the gas token; Mantle grew out of the BitDAO community.

detail.whatItIs: Mantle is a Layer 2 network for Ethereum that grew out of the BitDAO community, which merged into Mantle in 2023. People use it to run EVM apps, mainly decentralised finance, and pay fees in its own token, MNT, rather than in ETH. It began as an optimistic rollup and has since switched to zero-knowledge validity proofs, so it is now classed as a zk-rollup. MNT holders vote on governance proposals that steer the network and its treasury.
detail.howItWorks: Mantle runs a modified version of the OP Stack software. A sequencer orders transactions and posts the batch data to Ethereum as blobs; since the Arsia upgrade in April 2026 it no longer uses the separate EigenDA data network. Since September 2025, state updates are checked with OP Succinct, which uses the SP1 zero-knowledge virtual machine to prove that blocks were executed correctly. Ethereum verifies each proof, so withdrawals no longer wait about seven days for a challenge period to pass.

name: Taiko
summary: Ethereum-equivalent "based" rollup: blocks are ordered via Ethereum L1 and proven with several proofs, including ZK.
goodToKnow: "Based" means Ethereum L1 handles sequencing; as of November 2026, fast proposing is limited to whitelisted preconfirmers, with forced inclusion as a fallback.
Multi-proof: since the 2026 Unzen fork, each proven range needs two proofs from SGX (TEE), SP1 or RISC0, at least one of them a ZK proof.
The mainnet is called Taiko Alethia; ETH pays gas and TAIKO is the project's token.

detail.whatItIs: Taiko is a Layer 2 network for Ethereum whose mainnet, Taiko Alethia, launched in May 2024. It aims to be Ethereum-equivalent, so contracts, tools and node software from Ethereum run with minimal changes. It is a based rollup: instead of relying on its own central sequencer to order transactions, it lets Ethereum's block proposers settle the order. The aim is to inherit more of Ethereum's neutrality and resistance to downtime. ETH pays gas; TAIKO is the project's own token.
detail.howItWorks: Taiko blocks are proposed by submitting their data to a contract on Ethereum, so Ethereum's ordering becomes Taiko's ordering. Because Ethereum blocks come only every 12 seconds, approved preconfirmers can promise users faster inclusion in advance, and users can force transactions in through Ethereum if needed. Proofs come later and are checked on Ethereum. Taiko requires two different proofs for each proven range, at least one of them zero-knowledge, so a bug in a single proof system cannot on its own approve a false state.

name: Ink
summary: Ethereum optimistic rollup on the OP Stack, launched by the Kraken exchange.
goodToKnow: Ink is separate from Kraken's exchange: funds on Ink are in a self-custody wallet, not in a Kraken account balance.
Like other OP Stack chains, withdrawals to Ethereum rely on fault proofs and a challenge period (as of November 2026).
Mainnet launched in December 2024; it is one of the OP Stack chains in Optimism's Superchain.

detail.whatItIs: Ink is a Layer 2 network for Ethereum developed by the team at Kraken, the cryptocurrency exchange, with its mainnet live since December 2024. It is meant mainly for decentralised finance apps such as trading and lending. Ink is separate from Kraken's custodial exchange accounts: assets on Ink sit in wallets that users control themselves. It is an optimistic rollup built with the OP Stack and is one of the chains in Optimism's Superchain, which share standards and upgrades.
detail.howItWorks: Ink runs the standard OP Stack software. A sequencer orders transactions into blocks and posts the batch data to Ethereum. Proposed results, called state roots, are also published on Ethereum and treated as valid unless challenged. Anyone who believes a state root is wrong can open an on-chain dispute game, a fault proof that narrows the disagreement down to a single instruction which Ethereum then re-executes. Standard withdrawals to Ethereum therefore wait about seven days. As a Superchain member, Ink follows shared upgrades and security policies.

name: Aztec
summary: Privacy-focused Ethereum ZK rollup whose smart contracts can keep balances and data private, with proofs made on users' devices.
goodToKnow: As of November 2026 mainnet is in "Alpha": live with staking and user transactions, but called early, unaudited software. V6 ("Tierra") shipped in November 2026.
Contracts are written in Aztec.nr, based on the Noir language, not Solidity; it is not EVM-compatible.
Not the same as Aztec Connect, an earlier Aztec rollup that was shut down in 2024.

detail.whatItIs: Aztec is a Layer 2 network on Ethereum built for privacy. Its smart contracts can keep some data and balances private and other parts public, so an app could, for example, hide who holds a token while still publishing the total supply. Developers write contracts in Aztec.nr, based on the Noir language, rather than Solidity. As of November 2026 the mainnet runs as an Alpha with staking and user transactions, no component has been fully audited, and the Tierra (V6) upgrade launched on 3 November 2026.
detail.howItWorks: Private functions run on the user's own device, which produces a zero-knowledge proof that they ran correctly; the network sees only the proof and encrypted results. Private state is stored as notes, encrypted records, and spending one publishes a nullifier, a tag that prevents double spending without revealing which note was used. Public functions are executed by block proposers drawn from staked participants. Provers then combine the transactions of each epoch into one validity proof, which an Ethereum contract verifies before accepting the new state.

name: Degen Chain
summary: An Arbitrum Orbit L3 that settled on Base and used DEGEN for gas; it shut down on 31 August 2026.
goodToKnow: Kept on the map as an example: chains can shut down, and users must move assets off before bridges and RPC services are switched off.
The DEGEN token lives on Base and continues; the team wound down the chain to focus on social products in the Base ecosystem.
It had multi-day outages in 2024, a known risk for small chains that rely on a single operator.

detail.whatItIs: Degen Chain was a Layer 3 blockchain for the community around DEGEN, a tipping token created by users of the Farcaster social network. It launched in March 2024 and let DEGEN holders pay fees in DEGEN for cheap trades, memecoins and small apps. It settled on Base, Coinbase's Layer 2 network. The chain shut down on 31 August 2026, as the team chose to focus on social products in the Base ecosystem. The DEGEN token itself still exists on Base.
detail.howItWorks: Degen Chain was built with Arbitrum Orbit and operated by a single team through a hosted rollup provider. One sequencer ordered transactions and posted results to Base, where they could be challenged during a dispute window. DEGEN was bridged from Base to serve as the gas token. Because one operator ran the sequencer, any outage stopped the whole chain, as happened for several days in 2024. Before the shutdown, users had to bridge assets back to Base while bridges and RPC endpoints, the servers wallets use to reach a chain, were still running.

name: Compound
summary: Lending protocol where users supply crypto to earn interest and borrow against collateral, governed by COMP holders.
goodToKnow: The current version, Compound III ("Comet"), runs separate markets that each lend one base asset such as USDC, unlike v2's shared pools.
Loans are overcollateralised: if collateral value falls too far, the position is liquidated.
cTokens belong to the older Compound v2; v3 is deployed on Ethereum and several L2s (as of November 2026).

detail.whatItIs: Compound is a lending protocol: a set of smart contracts where people deposit crypto to earn interest and borrow other assets against collateral, without a bank or broker in between. It launched on Ethereum in 2018 and was one of the first on-chain money markets. The current version, Compound III, runs on Ethereum and several Layer 2 networks. Holders of the COMP token propose and vote on changes such as new markets, interest rate settings and collateral rules, which a timelock contract applies after a delay.
detail.howItWorks: Each Compound III market, called a Comet, has one base asset that can be borrowed, for example USDC, and a list of accepted collateral assets. Collateral only secures loans and does not earn interest. The interest rate rises as a larger share of the base asset is borrowed, following a curve set by governance. Each collateral asset has a collateral factor that caps how much can be borrowed against it, and prices come from oracles. If a borrower's debt passes the limit, anyone can trigger liquidation, and the protocol then sells the seized collateral at a discount.

name: Morpho
summary: Lending protocol made of isolated, permissionless markets, plus curated vaults that spread deposits across them.
goodToKnow: Each market pairs one collateral asset with one loan asset and fixed parameters, so risk stays isolated rather than pooled.
Vaults are managed by third-party curators who choose the markets; depositors take on the curator's risk choices.
Began as an optimiser on top of Aave and Compound before launching its own markets (Morpho Blue) in 2024; MORPHO is the governance token.

detail.whatItIs: Morpho is a lending protocol on Ethereum, Base and other EVM chains. Anyone can create a lending market without asking permission, and anyone can lend or borrow in it. Most depositors do not pick markets themselves: they put assets into vaults, whose curators decide where the money is lent. Apps and companies also build their own lending products with Morpho. MORPHO token holders govern the protocol through the Morpho DAO, which can change only a few things, such as fees and the list of allowed settings.
detail.howItWorks: A Morpho market is defined by five parameters: the loan asset, the collateral asset, a price oracle, an interest rate model and a liquidation loan-to-value (LLTV), the debt level at which a position can be liquidated. The rate model and LLTV are picked from a list approved by governance, and once a market exists nobody can change it. All markets live in one small core contract, which saves gas. Vaults sit above the markets and follow the ERC-4626 token-vault standard. As of January 2026, Vaults V2 can also allocate deposits to other Morpho versions, within caps the curator sets.

name: Pendle
summary: DeFi protocol that splits yield-bearing tokens into principal (PT) and yield (YT) tokens so future yield can be traded.
goodToKnow: Buying PT locks in a fixed yield until maturity; buying YT is a bet that the variable yield will be higher.
Users take on the underlying asset's risks plus smart-contract risk; YT is worth nothing after maturity.
PENDLE is the protocol's token; it is deployed on Ethereum and several other chains.

detail.whatItIs: Pendle is a DeFi protocol for trading future yield. Many tokens earn a yield, such as staked ETH or interest-bearing stablecoins. Pendle lets holders split such a token into two parts until a set maturity date: one that pays back the principal and one that collects the yield. Users can then lock in a fixed rate or speculate on how rates will move. It runs on Ethereum, Arbitrum and other chains. Since January 2026, PENDLE holders stake it as sPENDLE to vote and earn rewards, replacing the older vePENDLE locks.
detail.howItWorks: A yield-bearing token is first wrapped into a standard format called SY. SY is then split into a principal token (PT) and a yield token (YT) with the same maturity date. One PT can be redeemed for the underlying asset at maturity, so before then it trades at a discount; that discount is the fixed yield a buyer locks in. YT collects all the yield until maturity. Pendle's automated market maker trades PT against SY using a curve designed for assets whose prices converge over time, and YT trades go through the same pools using flash swaps.

sources.label: The Block: Pendle retires vePENDLE as sPENDLE staking goes live

name: Raydium
summary: Decentralised exchange on Solana that uses automated market makers (AMMs) for token swaps and liquidity pools.
goodToKnow: Offers standard constant-product pools and concentrated-liquidity pools; aggregators such as Jupiter often route trades through it.
Its LaunchLab lets anyone create and launch tokens; newly launched tokens carry high risk.
RAY is the protocol token.

detail.whatItIs: Raydium is a decentralised exchange (DEX) on Solana: a set of on-chain programs where people swap tokens without an intermediary holding their funds. Anyone can add tokens to a pool and earn a share of trading fees, and anyone can create a new pool for a token pair. Many swaps reach Raydium indirectly, through aggregators such as Jupiter. It also runs LaunchLab, a tool for launching new tokens. A core team develops it, and RAY is the protocol token.
detail.howItWorks: Raydium runs several pool types. Standard pools are automated market makers (AMMs) that follow the constant-product rule: the two token reserves multiplied together stay constant, so the price moves as one side is bought. Concentrated-liquidity pools let providers place their tokens within a chosen price range, so the same deposit supports more trading near the current price. Each swap pays a fee, most of which goes to liquidity providers and part to RAY buybacks and the treasury. LaunchLab tokens trade on a bonding curve, a formula-set price, until enough is raised, then move to a normal pool.

name: Jito
summary: Solana project offering the JitoSOL liquid-staking token and MEV infrastructure (a validator client and block engine).
goodToKnow: Its validator client lets searchers pay tips to get transaction bundles included; tips are shared with validators and their stakers.
JitoSOL represents staked SOL plus staking and MEV rewards; it carries smart-contract and validator risks.
JTO is the governance token; critics note that Jito's block engine concentrates part of Solana's MEV flow.

detail.whatItIs: Jito is a group of Solana projects built by Jito Labs and governed by the Jito DAO through the JTO token. For users, its main product is JitoSOL, a liquid staking token: deposit SOL, receive a token that earns staking rewards and can still be traded or used in DeFi. For validators and traders, it provides MEV infrastructure. MEV, maximal extractable value, is the profit available from choosing which transactions enter a block and in what order. Jito's tools turn that into an open auction.
detail.howItWorks: Jito-Solana, a modified validator client, accepts bundles: groups of transactions that must run together and in order. Searchers send bundles with a tip to Jito's block engine, which runs an auction and forwards the winning bundles to the validator that is producing blocks; tips are later shared with that validator's stakers. JitoSOL is a stake pool that spreads deposits across many validators, chosen by on-chain performance scores, and collects both staking rewards and MEV tips. Since September 2025, its Block Assembly Marketplace (BAM) has ordered transactions inside trusted hardware enclaves, so the ordering process can be verified.

sources.label: Jito Labs docs: low-latency transaction send
Blockworks: Jito launches BAM on Solana mainnet

name: Binance
summary: Centralised, custodial cryptocurrency exchange for trading, depositing and withdrawing crypto across many blockchains.
goodToKnow: Custodial: Binance holds users' keys, so funds there are an account balance, not self-custody.
BNB Chain grew out of Binance and BNB is that chain's token; the exchange and the chain are separate things.
In 2023 Binance and founder Changpeng Zhao pleaded guilty in the US to anti-money-laundering violations; he was pardoned in October 2025.

detail.whatItIs: Binance is a centralised crypto exchange founded in 2017. Users open an account, verify their identity and trade, stake, borrow or withdraw many cryptocurrencies, and it also offers futures and other derivatives. It operates through local entities in many countries, while some regions, including the US, are served by separate or restricted platforms. BNB Chain started as Binance's own chain and BNB is its token. Binance also owns Trust Wallet, a self-custody app separate from exchange accounts.
detail.howItWorks: Binance is custodial: it holds the keys for users' crypto in its own hot and cold wallets and records balances in an internal ledger. Trades are matched by its matching engine against central limit order books off-chain, so only deposits and withdrawals touch a blockchain. Fiat on-ramps and off-ramps use bank transfers, cards and peer-to-peer trading between users, depending on the country. Since July 2018 it has kept an emergency insurance fund called SAFU, and since November 2022 it publishes proof-of-reserves reports that let users check their balance in a Merkle tree.

name: Ethena (USDe)
summary: Protocol issuing USDe, a synthetic dollar backed by hedged crypto, loans and other assets, not by dollars in a bank.
goodToKnow: Core design: crypto such as ETH or BTC is paired with short perpetual/futures positions (delta-neutral). USDe is not backed by dollars in a bank.
As of November 2026 much of the backing has shifted to lending, stablecoins and tokenised assets; the mix changes over time and by governance.
Risks include negative funding rates, exchange or custodian failure and liquidity; sUSDe is the staked, yield-bearing version.

detail.whatItIs: Ethena is a protocol on Ethereum that issues USDe, a synthetic dollar: a token designed to hold a value of one dollar without being backed by dollars in a bank. Instead, it holds crypto and other assets whose price moves are offset by hedges. Holders can stake USDe to receive sUSDe, which earns a variable yield. Ethena Labs develops the protocol, and ENA is its governance token, used among other things to vote on the mix of backing assets.
detail.howItWorks: Approved, identity-checked institutions mint USDe by depositing assets and redeem it by returning USDe; other users buy it on markets. For volatile assets such as ETH or BTC, Ethena opens an equal short futures position on derivatives exchanges, so a fall in price is offset by a gain on the short: a delta-neutral position. These assets sit with custodians under off-exchange settlement rather than on the exchanges. Stablecoins, lending positions and tokenised real-world assets are held without hedging. sUSDe's yield comes from funding payments, staking rewards and interest, and drops when funding rates turn negative.

name: PYUSD (PayPal)
summary: US-dollar stablecoin issued by Paxos for PayPal, redeemable 1:1 and backed by dollar deposits and short-term US Treasuries.
goodToKnow: Paxos issues it and holds the reserves; PayPal brands it and offers it in its apps (launched August 2023).
Issued natively on Ethereum, Solana and other chains (as of November 2026); bridged versions on other chains are different tokens.
Centrally issued: the issuer can freeze tokens held at specific addresses.

detail.whatItIs: PayPal USD, or PYUSD, is a dollar stablecoin that PayPal launched in August 2023. Paxos, a regulated trust company, issues it and holds the reserves; PayPal brands it and lets customers buy, hold, send and pay with it in the PayPal and Venmo apps. Each token is meant to be worth one US dollar. Outside PayPal it works like any other token: it can be held in self-custody wallets and used in DeFi apps on the chains where it is issued.
detail.howItWorks: Paxos mints PYUSD when dollars are deposited and burns it on redemption, at one dollar per token. Reserves are held in dollar deposits, short-term US Treasuries and similar cash equivalents, with monthly reserve reports. Paxos Trust Company is supervised by the New York State Department of Financial Services, and in December 2025 Paxos also received conditional approval for a US national trust bank charter. Issuance is native on Ethereum, Solana and other chains including Arbitrum and Polygon (as of November 2026), while PYUSD0 on further chains is a separate bridged version built with LayerZero.

sources.label: PayPal newsroom: PYUSD expands to Arbitrum (July 2025)
The Block: PYUSD native issuance on Polygon (2026)

name: EURC (Circle)
summary: Euro stablecoin issued by Circle, redeemable 1:1 for euros and backed by euro-denominated reserves.
goodToKnow: Issued under the EU's MiCA rules by Circle's French entity (as of November 2026); it was formerly called Euro Coin (EUROC).
Issued natively on Ethereum, Solana, Avalanche, Base and other chains; it is a separate token from USDC.
Centrally issued: Circle can freeze tokens held at specific addresses.

detail.whatItIs: EURC is a euro stablecoin issued by Circle, the company behind USDC. Each token is meant to be worth one euro and can be redeemed for one by Circle's eligible customers. It lets people and companies hold, send and settle euros on public blockchains, for example for cross-border payments or trading pairs priced in euros. It launched in June 2022 under the name Euro Coin (EUROC). It is a separate token from USDC, with its own reserves.
detail.howItWorks: Circle mints EURC when eligible customers deposit euros and burns it when they redeem, one for one. The reserves are euro-denominated, held as cash at banks and in short-term holdings, and Circle publishes reserve attestations. Since July 2024 EURC has been issued in the EU under MiCA, the Markets in Crypto-Assets regulation, by Circle Internet Financial Europe SAS, an electronic money institution licensed by the ACPR, France's banking supervisor. Under MiCA, holders have a right to redeem at par, and a minimum share of reserves must be kept as bank deposits.

sources.label: Circle developer docs: what is EURC

name: Ledger
summary: Company making hardware wallets: devices that keep private keys offline and sign transactions for many blockchains.
goodToKnow: The device holds the keys; the Ledger Wallet app (formerly Ledger Live) or wallets like MetaMask show balances and prepare transactions.
Anyone with the 24-word recovery phrase can take the funds; Ledger never asks for it.
A 2020 customer-database leak exposed buyers' contact details and led to phishing; it did not expose keys.

detail.whatItIs: Ledger is a French company, founded in 2014, that makes hardware wallets, which it now calls signers: small devices such as the Nano and Stax that keep private keys away from internet-connected computers and phones. Users pair the device with the Ledger Wallet app, called Ledger Live until October 2025, or with other wallets such as MetaMask, to see balances and prepare transactions for Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana and many other networks. Each blockchain needs its own small app installed on the device.
detail.howItWorks: At setup, the device generates the keys inside a secure element, a tamper-resistant chip of the kind used in bank cards, and displays a 24-word recovery phrase for the user to write down. Keys never leave the chip. The app on a computer or phone builds an unsigned transaction and sends it to the device by USB or Bluetooth. The device shows the recipient and amount on its own screen; the user confirms with a button or touch, and the chip signs. Clear Signing, based on the ERC-7730 format, shows smart contract actions in readable form.

sources.label: Ledger press release: Nano Gen5 and Ledger Wallet (October 2025)

name: Trust Wallet
summary: Self-custody mobile and browser wallet for many blockchains, owned by Binance.
goodToKnow: Self-custody: keys stay on the user's device, so losing the recovery phrase means losing access.
Owned by Binance since 2018, but funds in Trust Wallet sit on-chain in the user's addresses, not in a Binance account.
In December 2025 a malicious Chrome extension update (v2.68) drained some users' wallets; the mobile app was not affected.

detail.whatItIs: Trust Wallet is a self-custody wallet app for phones, with a browser extension, that supports many blockchains, including Ethereum, BNB Chain, Solana and Bitcoin. People use it to store tokens and NFTs, swap, stake and connect to decentralised apps through its built-in browser and WalletConnect. Binance acquired it in 2018, but funds in Trust Wallet sit in the user's own addresses, not in a Binance account. TWT is its token, used for in-app benefits and governance votes.
detail.howItWorks: On setup the app generates a recovery phrase, usually 12 words, and derives a key for each chain from it using its open-source Wallet Core library. Keys are encrypted and stored on the device; Trust Wallet's servers do not hold them, so the company cannot move funds or restore a lost phrase. When the user approves a transfer or a request from an app, the wallet signs on the device and broadcasts the transaction through a node. Because the extension keeps keys inside the browser, a malicious extension update, as in December 2025, can expose them.

sources.label: Trust Wallet: v2.68 extension incident update

name: Polymarket
summary: Prediction market where users trade shares on real-world events, settled in pUSD, a USDC-backed token, on Polygon PoS.
goodToKnow: Prices reflect traders' bets, not certainties; markets are resolved through UMA's optimistic oracle, and some outcomes have been disputed.
Access depends on the country; in the US it runs a separate, CFTC-regulated platform (as of November 2026).
As of November 2026 it runs on Polygon PoS; it has said it plans to move to another chain.

detail.whatItIs: Polymarket is a prediction market: users buy and sell shares that pay out one dollar if an event happens, such as an election result, and nothing if it does not. A share's price, between zero and one dollar, reflects what traders collectively expect. Founded in 2020, it runs on Polygon PoS and, since its V2 upgrade in April 2026, uses pUSD, its own USDC-backed token, for trading. In the US it runs a separate platform regulated by the CFTC, the derivatives regulator.
detail.howItWorks: Each market has YES and NO outcome tokens created with the Conditional Token Framework: one pUSD can be split into one YES and one NO, and a full pair merged back. Users sign orders that Polymarket's operator matches off-chain in a central limit order book; the exchange contract on Polygon then settles each trade on-chain, and the operator cannot set prices or trade without a user's signature. After the event, UMA's optimistic oracle reports the result: a proposed answer stands unless disputed, in which case UMA token holders vote. Winning tokens redeem for one pUSD each.

name: Farcaster
summary: Decentralised social network protocol: accounts are registered on-chain and posts are stored on its own network (Snapchain).
goodToKnow: Account IDs (FIDs) are registered in contracts on OP Mainnet; posts and other messages are kept off Ethereum on Snapchain.
Many apps (clients) can read the same accounts and posts; the main app was formerly called Warpcast.
Ownership changed twice in 2026: Neynar acquired it in January, then Network School in October (as of November 2026).

detail.whatItIs: Farcaster is a protocol for a decentralised social network: accounts, posts, follows and likes live on a shared network that many apps can read and write, so users can switch apps without losing their followers. Its main app was formerly called Warpcast. Posts can embed mini apps, formerly called Frames, small interactive programs. The founding team at Merkle Manufactory sold it to Neynar in January 2026, and Network School, founded by Balaji Srinivasan, acquired it in October 2026.
detail.howItWorks: Each account gets a Farcaster ID (FID) from a registry contract on OP Mainnet, an Ethereum layer 2, owned by the user's Ethereum address. The owner authorises app keys, also recorded on OP Mainnet, so apps can post on the user's behalf. Posts and reactions are messages signed with those keys and stored on Snapchain, a separate network where validators order messages into blocks using Tendermint-style consensus that tolerates up to one third faulty validators. Storage units bought on-chain limit how much each account can keep. Anyone can run a node to read the data.

name: Infura
summary: Hosted node service from Consensys that lets apps and wallets read and send blockchain data without running their own nodes.
goodToKnow: MetaMask uses Infura by default for many networks, so an Infura outage or policy change can affect MetaMask users.
Using a provider means trusting it for correct data and uptime; it can also see request metadata such as IP addresses.
As of November 2026 its documentation is published under MetaMask's developer services.

detail.whatItIs: Infura is a hosted node service run by Consensys, the company that also makes the MetaMask wallet. It lets wallets and apps read blockchain data and broadcast transactions over the internet without running their own nodes. It supports Ethereum and many other networks, including Linea and several Layer 2 rollups. Because MetaMask uses it by default, many users depend on Infura without knowing it. In November 2025 Consensys launched the Decentralized Infrastructure Network (DIN) as an EigenLayer service, to spread request handling across independent providers.
detail.howItWorks: Infura runs clusters of blockchain nodes behind a load balancer. Developers create an API key and send standard JSON-RPC requests, such as reading a balance or submitting a signed transaction, to an Infura endpoint. Plans are metered by request credits, with a free tier. Through DIN, some requests are routed to independent partner node providers, which adds redundancy. DIN runs as an actively validated service on EigenLayer: restaked ETH backs the network's operators and watchers, giving them a financial reason to report and serve data honestly.

sources.label: Consensys blog: DIN launches as EigenLayer AVS

name: Hardhat
summary: Development environment for compiling, testing, deploying and debugging Ethereum smart contracts, built in TypeScript.
goodToKnow: Runs a local Ethereum network for testing; tests are often written in TypeScript, and Hardhat 3 also supports tests written in Solidity.
Maintained by the Nomic Foundation, a non-profit.
A developer tool, not a blockchain or a wallet; it is often compared with Foundry.

detail.whatItIs: Hardhat is a free, open-source development environment for smart contracts on Ethereum and other EVM chains. Developers use it on their own computer to compile Solidity code, run automated tests, debug failed transactions and deploy contracts to test networks or mainnet. It is maintained by the Nomic Foundation, a non-profit. Hardhat 3, released in 2025, is described by its documentation as stable and production-ready, and Hardhat 2 has an announced end-of-life date. It is a tool on a developer's machine, not a network.
detail.howItWorks: A project has a configuration file, written in TypeScript, that lists compiler versions, networks and plugins. Hardhat downloads the right Solidity compiler and builds the contracts. For testing it runs a simulated Ethereum network in memory, powered by EDR, a runtime written in Rust; it produces stack traces and supports console.log calls inside Solidity. Tests can be written in TypeScript with libraries such as viem or ethers, or, since Hardhat 3, in Solidity. Hardhat Ignition describes deployments as modules, so an interrupted deployment can resume where it stopped. Plugins add tasks such as contract verification.

sources.label: Hardhat docs: what's new in Hardhat 3

name: Foundry
summary: Command-line toolkit written in Rust for building, testing and deploying EVM smart contracts, with tests written in Solidity.
goodToKnow: Includes forge (build and test), cast (interact with chains), anvil (local node) and chisel (Solidity shell).
Tests, including fuzz tests, are written in Solidity itself; it is often compared with Hardhat.
Open source, started at Paradigm; version 1.0 was released in 2025.

detail.whatItIs: Foundry is a free, open-source toolkit for smart contract developers working on Ethereum and other EVM chains. It runs from the command line and is written in Rust, which makes compiling and testing fast. Its main idea is that tests and deployment scripts are written in Solidity, the same language as the contracts, so developers do not need to switch to JavaScript or TypeScript. It was started at Paradigm, a crypto investment firm, in 2021 and is developed in the open on GitHub.
detail.howItWorks: forge compiles contracts and runs tests. Each test is a Solidity function, and special functions called cheatcodes let a test change the block time, act as another address or expect a call to fail. Fuzz tests run a function with many random inputs, and invariant tests call contracts in random sequences to check that a rule always holds. Forge can also fork a live chain, fetching its state on demand from a node, so tests run against real deployed contracts. anvil runs a local node, cast reads chain data and sends transactions, and chisel is an interactive Solidity shell.

name: Chronicle
summary: Oracle network that grew out of MakerDAO's oracle team; it supplies price feeds to Sky (formerly MakerDAO) and others.
goodToKnow: Its Scribe oracle contracts use Schnorr signatures so many validators' signatures can be checked cheaply on-chain.
Feeds are signed by a known set of validators (e.g. Bitcoin Suisse, Steakhouse Financial), so users trust that group.
Reading many feeds requires being whitelisted; it also offers proof-of-asset data for tokenised real-world assets (as of November 2026).

detail.whatItIs: Chronicle is an oracle network that started inside MakerDAO, now Sky, which needed reliable collateral prices for the vaults behind its stablecoins. It became a separate company, Chronicle Labs, in 2023 and still supplies Sky's price feeds, as well as feeds for other protocols on Ethereum and several Layer 2s. Beyond crypto prices, it publishes proof-of-asset data that shows the backing of tokenised real-world assets, as of November 2026. Reading many of its feeds requires being whitelisted.
detail.howItWorks: A known set of validators, organisations such as Bitcoin Suisse and Steakhouse Financial, each sign the latest price off-chain. The Scribe contract then accepts one update carrying an aggregated Schnorr signature, a single signature that combines many signers' keys, so checking it costs far less gas than verifying each signature separately. An optimistic variant, ScribeOptimistic, stores updates without the full check and lets anyone prove an invalid signature during a short challenge window, which removes the bad value. Each value records which validators signed it, so its origin can be checked.

name: RedStone
summary: Modular oracle that delivers signed price data to many chains, either pushed on-chain or pulled into transactions on demand.
goodToKnow: Pull model: prices are signed off-chain and attached to the user's transaction, which saves gas but needs app integration.
Provides feeds for newer assets such as liquid-restaking tokens; RED is its token (as of November 2026).
Any oracle means trusting its data providers and signers: wrong prices can trigger wrong liquidations.

detail.whatItIs: RedStone is an oracle network that delivers price data to smart contracts on many chains. It is modular: an app can have prices pushed on-chain at regular intervals like a classic oracle, or pull signed prices into its own transactions only when needed. It also covers newer assets such as liquid staking and restaking tokens, and lending and derivatives protocols use it to value collateral and positions. RED is its token, as of November 2026. RedStone was founded in 2020.
detail.howItWorks: Independent data providers fetch prices from exchanges and aggregators, sign them, and broadcast these signed data packages to off-chain gateways, so nothing is written on-chain until it is needed. In the pull model, called RedStone Core, the app's front end attaches the latest packages to the user's transaction, and the contract checks that enough authorised signers agree before using the price. In the push model, called Classic, relayers write prices to on-chain feed contracts when the price moves beyond a threshold or a set time has passed.

name: Dune
summary: Analytics platform where people query indexed blockchain data with SQL and share dashboards.
goodToKnow: Dashboards are made by users; each query has its own assumptions, so the same metric can differ between dashboards.
Data from many chains is decoded and indexed; free use has limits, and an API is available.
An analytics tool, not an oracle: smart contracts cannot read Dune data directly.

detail.whatItIs: Dune is an analytics website where anyone can query blockchain data using SQL, the common database query language, and turn the results into charts and dashboards. Researchers, journalists, protocol teams and investors use it to answer questions such as how many addresses used an app last month. Public dashboards can be copied and adapted by others. Dune is a company, not a protocol: basic use is free within limits, and it charges for heavier usage, private queries and its data API.
detail.howItWorks: Dune collects blocks, transactions, event logs and traces from many chains into raw tables. When someone submits a contract's ABI, the description of its functions and events, Dune decodes that contract's activity into readable tables. An open-source project called Spellbook, maintained with the community, builds curated tables such as dex.trades that standardise similar data across protocols and chains. Queries run on DuneSQL, an engine based on Trino, and results can be charted, refreshed on a schedule, or fetched by other programs through the API.

name: Arkham
summary: Blockchain analytics platform that labels addresses with real-world entities and lets users track fund flows.
goodToKnow: Labels come from its own analysis and user submissions; attributions can be wrong and should be double-checked.
Its "Intel Exchange" lets users post bounties for identifying addresses, which raised privacy concerns.
Arkham also launched a crypto exchange in 2024; in February 2026 it was reported to be winding down, which Arkham called a move to a DEX.

detail.whatItIs: Arkham is a blockchain analytics platform run by the company Arkham Intelligence. It attaches real-world names to addresses, such as exchanges, funds, governments or individuals, and lets users follow funds between them on chains including Ethereum and Bitcoin. Journalists, traders and investigators use it to see, for example, where stolen funds moved. Basic use on its website is free. Its Intel Exchange lets people offer or earn bounties, paid in the ARKM token, for identifying who controls an address.
detail.howItWorks: Arkham indexes several blockchains and groups addresses into entities with an attribution engine it calls Ultra, which combines on-chain patterns, such as addresses that repeatedly fund each other, with public information and user submissions. On the Intel Exchange, a buyer posts a bounty for an address or entity, a seller submits evidence, and Arkham reviews it before the bounty is paid and the label may be published. The Visualizer draws fund flows as a graph, and alerts notify users when watched addresses move funds.

name: Chainalysis
summary: Blockchain analytics company whose tools trace funds and flag risky addresses for governments, exchanges and investigators.
goodToKnow: Its software (e.g. Reactor, KYT) is used for compliance and law-enforcement investigations, such as tracing stolen funds.
Attribution relies on clustering heuristics and intelligence; it is powerful but not infallible, and its methods have been challenged in court.
A private company, not a protocol and without a token.

detail.whatItIs: Chainalysis is a private company, founded in 2014, that sells blockchain analysis software. Government agencies, law enforcement, exchanges and banks use it to trace where crypto funds came from and where they went, to check whether a customer's deposit is linked to risky sources such as sanctioned addresses or stolen funds, and to support criminal investigations. Its main products include Reactor, for investigations, and KYT, short for Know Your Transaction, for monitoring. It also publishes research reports on crypto crime.
detail.howItWorks: Chainalysis reads the public ledgers of many blockchains and groups addresses into clusters believed to belong to one entity, using heuristics such as common-input ownership: the assumption that all inputs of one Bitcoin transaction belong to the same owner. It then attaches names to clusters using information from services, open sources, investigations and its own test transactions. Reactor lets investigators draw and follow fund flows as graphs. KYT screens an exchange's deposits and withdrawals as they happen and alerts compliance teams to exposure to risky sources.

name: Axelar
summary: Cross-chain network with its own proof-of-stake validators that passes messages and tokens between blockchains.
goodToKnow: Built with the Cosmos SDK; its validators jointly sign cross-chain messages, so security depends on that validator set.
Offers general message passing (GMP) and an Interchain Token Service; AXL is the staking token.
Circle agreed in December 2025 to acquire the Interop Labs team; the network and AXL stayed independent, with Common Prefix taking a lead role.

detail.whatItIs: Axelar is a cross-chain network: a blockchain of its own whose job is to pass messages and tokens between other blockchains, such as Ethereum, its Layer 2s and Cosmos chains. Developers use its general message passing (GMP) to call a contract on another chain, and its Interchain Token Service to issue tokens that exist on several chains. Tokens it bridges often carry an axl prefix, such as axlUSDC. In December 2025 Circle agreed to acquire the Interop Labs team that built it, while the network itself stayed independent.
detail.howItWorks: Axelar is a proof-of-stake chain built with the Cosmos SDK, and it deploys gateway contracts on each connected chain. When an app sends a message, the source gateway emits an event. Axelar validators each watch that chain and vote that the event happened; once validators holding enough stake agree, they sign an approval that the destination gateway accepts. A relayer then delivers the message and executes the call. Because the validators' signatures authorise everything, the bridge is only as safe as that validator set, which AXL holders choose by staking.

name: Across
summary: Intent-based bridge where relayers front funds on the destination chain and are repaid later after verification.
goodToKnow: Users receive funds quickly because a relayer pays them up front; relayers carry the delay and risk until they are repaid.
Repayments are checked through UMA's optimistic oracle, which can be disputed during a challenge window.
ACX is the protocol token; it moves assets mainly between Ethereum, its L2s and other chains.

detail.whatItIs: Across is a bridge for moving tokens between Ethereum, its Layer 2 networks such as Arbitrum and Base, and other chains. It is intent-based: the user states the outcome they want, for example 100 USDC arriving on Base, and a third party called a relayer delivers it from its own funds, usually within seconds. The relayer is repaid later from a shared pool. ACX is the protocol token, used to vote in the DAO that governs the protocol's settings.
detail.howItWorks: A user deposits tokens into an Across spoke pool contract on the origin chain. Relayers watch these deposits and compete to fill them by sending their own tokens to the user on the destination chain. Periodically a proposer bundles all fills and proposes repaying the relayers from a hub pool on Ethereum. The bundle goes through UMA's optimistic oracle: it is accepted unless someone disputes it within a challenge window, in which case UMA token holders vote. Liquidity providers fund the hub pool and earn fees in return.

name: Hyperlane
summary: Permissionless interoperability protocol: anyone can deploy it to a chain and send messages and tokens between chains.
goodToKnow: Each app chooses its own security setup (Interchain Security Modules), so safety varies from one deployment to another.
Warp Routes move tokens between chains, using lock-and-mint or burn-and-mint designs.
Formerly called Abacus; HYPER is its token (launched 2025).

detail.whatItIs: Hyperlane is an interoperability protocol: software that lets blockchains send messages and tokens to each other. It is permissionless, meaning anyone can deploy its contracts to a new chain without asking the Hyperlane team, so newer chains and rollups can connect themselves. Apps use it to call contracts on other chains, and Warp Routes are its ready-made token bridges. It supports EVM chains, chains using Solana's virtual machine and Cosmos chains. It was formerly called Abacus, and HYPER is its token, launched in 2025.
detail.howItWorks: On each chain a Mailbox contract sends and receives messages. Off-chain relayers carry messages between Mailboxes, but a message is only delivered if the receiving app's Interchain Security Module (ISM) accepts it. The default module asks a set of validators to sign checkpoints of the source chain's outgoing messages, and a message passes once a threshold of them, such as three of five, has signed. Apps can instead require other proofs, combine several modules or appoint their own validators. Warp Routes either lock tokens and mint copies, or burn and re-mint them.

name: CCTP (Circle)
summary: Circle's Cross-Chain Transfer Protocol: it burns USDC on one chain and mints native USDC on another, with no wrapped tokens.
goodToKnow: Circle signs an attestation for each burn, so users trust Circle, the USDC issuer, rather than a third-party bridge.
CCTP V2 adds faster transfers and hooks; the older V1 is being deprecated, with a full pause scheduled for 1 December 2026.
It only moves Circle-issued tokens such as USDC, not arbitrary assets.

detail.whatItIs: CCTP, the Cross-Chain Transfer Protocol, is Circle's own system for moving USDC between blockchains. Rather than locking USDC in a bridge and issuing a wrapped copy, it destroys the tokens on one chain and creates the same amount of native USDC on the other, so total supply is unchanged and no IOU is left behind. Wallets, exchanges and other bridges call it in the background. It works on chains where Circle issues native USDC, such as Ethereum, Solana, Base and Avalanche.
detail.howItWorks: An app calls a CCTP contract that burns USDC on the source chain and records the destination and recipient. Circle's off-chain attestation service, Iris, sees the burn, waits for the required block confirmations and signs a message approving it. Anyone can submit that signed message to the destination chain's contract, which checks Circle's signature and mints the USDC. In V2, a Standard Transfer waits for finality, about 15 to 19 minutes from Ethereum, while a paid Fast Transfer completes in seconds. Hooks let the arriving funds trigger a follow-up action automatically.

name: ether.fi
summary: Liquid staking protocol: users stake ETH and receive eETH or weETH; restaking is a separate opt-in token built on Symbiotic.
goodToKnow: The liquid tokens keep staked ETH usable in DeFi, but add smart-contract, slashing and depeg risks on top of staking.
Began as a liquid restaking protocol on EigenLayer; in 2026 it wound that position down (under 1% left by August 2026).
Also offers a crypto-backed payment card and other "neobank" products (as of November 2026).

detail.whatItIs: ether.fi is an app on Ethereum for liquid staking: users deposit ETH and receive eETH, or its wrapped form weETH, tokens that represent the staked ETH and can still be used in DeFi, the open lending and trading apps built on blockchains. It began as a liquid restaking protocol built around EigenLayer, but as of November 2026 restaking is a separate opt-in product. The company also offers a crypto-backed payment card and other neobank-style services. ETHFI holders vote on governance.
detail.howItWorks: Deposited ETH is staked through Ethereum validators run by node operators that ether.fi works with. eETH is a rebasing token: its balance grows as staking rewards arrive. weETH keeps a fixed balance while each unit becomes worth more eETH. ether.fi's docs say that by August 2026 less than 1% of protocol assets was still restaked on EigenLayer, with the rest due to be removed by the end of 2026. Users who want restaking now opt into a separate token, weETHs, built with Symbiotic. Redemptions to ETH depend on available liquidity and validator withdrawals.

name: Symbiotic
summary: Permissionless restaking protocol on Ethereum where networks can be secured by many kinds of staked ERC-20 collateral.
goodToKnow: Unlike EigenLayer's ETH-first start, it accepts many ERC-20 assets as collateral, with vaults setting their own rules.
Restaked collateral can be slashed if operators misbehave, adding risk on top of the asset's own risks.
Networks that use it for "shared security" pay operators and stakers rewards in return.

detail.whatItIs: Symbiotic is a restaking protocol on Ethereum. Restaking means reusing assets that already secure one system as security for others, earning extra rewards in exchange for extra risk. Networks that need economic security, such as oracles, bridges or new chains, can obtain it from Symbiotic stakers instead of building their own validator set. Anyone can create a vault or launch a network without permission. It is a set of smart contracts rather than its own chain, and it is an alternative to EigenLayer.
detail.howItWorks: Three roles meet in Symbiotic's contracts. Vaults hold the deposited collateral, which can be any ERC-20 token, and their curators decide which operators receive stake and for which networks. Operators run the software each network requires. Networks define the rules, pay rewards and, through their middleware contract, can ask a vault to slash an operator's stake for misbehaviour. Vaults and networks agree in advance on slashing limits and on optional resolvers, parties that can veto an unfair slashing request. Because one stake may back several networks, slashing on one network reduces security for the others.

name: Avail
summary: Data availability blockchain, built with the Polkadot SDK, where rollups can publish their data instead of on Ethereum.
goodToKnow: Uses KZG commitments and data availability sampling, so light clients can check that data was published without downloading all of it.
Spun out of Polygon in 2023; AVAIL is its staking token.
Rollups using it rely on Avail's validators, not Ethereum, to keep their data available.

detail.whatItIs: Avail is a separate blockchain specialised in data availability: guaranteeing that the transaction data a rollup publishes can be downloaded by anyone who needs to check it. A rollup, a chain that posts its transactions to another chain, can publish that data on Avail instead of Ethereum, usually at lower cost. Avail started inside Polygon and became an independent project in 2023. Its token, AVAIL, is staked to secure the chain. The team also builds Nexus, a product for coordinating assets and activity across chains.
detail.howItWorks: Avail is built with Substrate, the framework of the Polkadot SDK, and uses nominated proof of stake: token holders back validators, BABE picks who produces each block and GRANDPA finalises them. Blocks arrive about every 20 seconds. Each block's data is arranged in a grid, extended with erasure coding so it can be rebuilt from part of it, and committed to with KZG commitments, short cryptographic fingerprints. Light clients download a few random cells and check them against those commitments. If enough samples verify, the whole block is very likely available.

name: Railgun
summary: Privacy system on EVM chains that lets users hold and use tokens in a shielded balance, using zero-knowledge proofs.
goodToKnow: Runs as smart contracts on Ethereum, Polygon, Arbitrum and BNB Chain; it is not a separate blockchain.
"Private Proofs of Innocence" aim to keep funds from known illicit sources out of the shielded pool.
It does not guarantee anonymity: timing and amounts can still link transactions.

detail.whatItIs: Railgun is a privacy system that runs as smart contracts on Ethereum, Polygon, Arbitrum and BNB Chain. Users move tokens into a shielded balance, then can send them, swap them on decentralised exchanges or use other DeFi apps without revealing their address, balance or the amounts involved. Wallets such as Railway build it in. It is governed by a DAO whose members vote with the RAIL token. A screening system called Private Proofs of Innocence aims to keep funds from known illicit sources out.
detail.howItWorks: Shielding deposits tokens into the Railgun contract and records an encrypted note, a private record of ownership, in a Merkle tree, a structure that summarises many records in one hash. To spend, the wallet builds a Groth16 zk-SNARK proof showing it owns unspent notes of enough value without revealing which ones. The contract verifies the proof and records nullifiers so notes cannot be spent twice. Independent broadcasters can submit the transaction and take their fee from the shielded balance, so the user's public address never appears. Unshielding returns tokens to a public address.
